q: You have a Microsoft Entra tenant with 5,000 users. A Conditional Access policy must apply to everyone in the Sales department, including people who transfer into Sales later. You need a group the policy can target. The solution must minimize administrative effort. What should you create?
opts: A security group with dynamic user membership based on the department attribute
A Microsoft 365 group with assigned membership, populated by a scheduled PowerShell script
An administrative unit that contains the Sales department users
A security group with assigned membership and group-based licensing enabled
why: A dynamic membership rule such as user.department -eq "Sales" is re-evaluated automatically whenever the attribute changes, and Conditional Access can target a security group directly. A script-populated assigned group reaches the same end state but is plumbing you must schedule, monitor, and fix. An administrative unit scopes Microsoft Entra role assignments to a subset of users; a Conditional Access policy cannot target an administrative unit. Group-based licensing hands licenses to whoever is already a member; it does nothing to decide who the members are.

q: You assign Microsoft 365 E3 to Group1 through group-based licensing. User1, a member of Group1, also has E3 assigned directly from before the group existed. You need User1's license to be managed only through Group1, with no interruption to User1's mailbox or apps. What should you do?
opts: Remove the direct E3 assignment from User1
Remove User1 from Group1, wait for the license to release, then add User1 back
Run Reprocess on Group1 to replace the direct assignment with the inherited one
Convert Group1 to a dynamic group so inherited licenses take precedence over direct ones
why: A directly assigned license and a group-inherited license for the same product coexist on the user, so removing the direct one simply leaves the inherited one in force with no gap in service. Removing and re-adding the user from the group never touches the direct assignment and risks a brief interruption. Reprocess only re-evaluates the group's own assignments; it does not remove direct assignments. Dynamic membership changes how members are selected, not how direct and inherited licenses are reconciled.

q: Contoso needs 40 consultants from Fabrikam to access a SharePoint site and one Azure resource group. The consultants must authenticate with their Fabrikam credentials, Contoso must not store or reset their passwords, and Fabrikam's IT department will not take part in the setup. What should you do?
opts: Invite each consultant as a guest user through Microsoft Entra External Identities
Configure cross-tenant synchronization between the Fabrikam and Contoso tenants
Create cloud-only member accounts for the consultants and require MFA at first sign-in
Create a Microsoft Entra External ID customer tenant and register the consultants in it
why: A B2B invitation creates a guest object that the consultant redeems with their Fabrikam credentials, so Contoso never holds a password, and the guest can then be granted SharePoint and Azure RBAC access like any other identity. Cross-tenant synchronization also produces B2B users, but it must be configured in the source tenant by Fabrikam's administrators, which the scenario rules out. Member accounts mean Contoso owns and resets those passwords. An External ID customer tenant serves consumer-facing apps and does not grant access to Contoso's internal SharePoint or Azure resources.

q: Your hybrid environment syncs on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID. Self-service password reset is enabled and users complete resets successfully, but afterwards the new password only works for cloud apps; signing in to a domain-joined PC still requires the old password. What should you configure?
opts: Password writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect
Password hash synchronization in Microsoft Entra Connect
Pass-through authentication with an additional authentication agent
Seamless single sign-on for the synchronized users
why: SSPR changes the cloud password; password writeback is the component that pushes that change back into on-premises Active Directory so domain sign-in matches. Password hash synchronization flows the other direction, on-premises to cloud, and would never carry a cloud-initiated reset downward. Pass-through authentication validates sign-ins against on-premises AD, so without writeback it would make the new password fail everywhere rather than fix it. Seamless SSO suppresses sign-in prompts on domain-joined devices and does not synchronize credentials at all.

q: A user is assigned Contributor at the subscription level and Owner at one specific resource group within it. What's their effective permission in that resource group?
opts: Contributor
No access
Reader
Owner
why: RBAC assignments are additive across scopes, and the more permissive assignment applies — Owner at that resource group wins there. Conflicting scopes don't cancel each other out into no access; the broader Contributor assignment from the subscription simply gets overridden by the more permissive Owner role at the narrower scope.

q: User1 must be able to grant colleagues access to resource group RG1, but must not be able to create, modify, or delete any resource in RG1. You need to assign a role to User1. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. Which role assignment should you create?
opts: User Access Administrator at the RG1 scope
Owner at the RG1 scope
Contributor at the RG1 scope plus Reader at the subscription scope
The Privileged Role Administrator Microsoft Entra role
why: User Access Administrator grants Microsoft.Authorization/* for managing role assignments plus read access, and nothing that lets User1 change the resources themselves. Owner would satisfy the first requirement but hands over full resource management too. Contributor explicitly excludes Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write, so User1 could not grant access at all, and layering Reader on top changes nothing. Privileged Role Administrator is a directory role for managing Microsoft Entra role assignments; it carries no Azure RBAC permission on RG1.

q: Your subscription has 200 resource groups. New resources must carry both a CostCenter and an Environment tag, and the compliance view must report one overall percentage for the tagging standard. You also want to add a third tag rule later without creating another assignment. What should you create?
opts: An initiative containing a require-tag policy per tag, assigned once at the subscription
Two separate policy assignments at the subscription, one per tag
One policy assignment with the Modify effect that inherits both tags from the resource group
A tag on each resource group, applied through the Tags blade
why: An initiative is the construct that gives you a single assignment and a single aggregated compliance score across several definitions, and adding a definition to the initiative later flows through the existing assignment. Two separate assignments report separately and would need a third assignment for the next tag. A Modify policy that inherits from the resource group copies tags rather than requiring them, so resources in untagged groups stay untagged, and it is still a single policy rather than a standard. Tagging each group by hand enforces nothing on the resources inside.

q: User1 has Reader at management group MG1 and Contributor at subscription Sub1 beneath it. Sub1 contains RG1 and nine other resource groups. You must ensure User1 can only read RG1 while keeping Contributor access to the other nine resource groups. What should you do?
opts: Remove Contributor at Sub1 and assign it at each of the other nine resource groups
Assign User1 the Reader role at the RG1 scope so the narrower scope applies
Create a deny assignment for User1 at the RG1 scope in Access control (IAM)
Apply a ReadOnly management lock at the RG1 scope
why: RBAC is additive, so a narrower assignment can never subtract rights inherited from a wider one; the only way to carve RG1 out is to move Contributor down to the nine scopes where it is wanted, after which the inherited Reader from MG1 is all that applies in RG1. Assigning Reader at RG1 changes nothing because Contributor still flows down from Sub1. Deny assignments cannot be authored directly by administrators; they are created by deployment stacks (the successor to Azure Blueprints, which retires on January 31, 2027) and managed applications. A ReadOnly lock would make RG1 read-only for every principal, not just User1.

q: Assigning the Reader role at a resource group to a user who already holds Contributor at the parent subscription restricts that user to read-only access inside the resource group.
opts: True
False
why: Role assignments are additive across scopes and the most permissive applicable assignment wins, so the inherited Contributor still applies in that resource group and the extra Reader assignment is redundant. Narrowing someone's access means removing or moving the broader assignment, not stacking a smaller one beneath it.

q: A user who holds the Contributor role at the subscription scope can assign the Reader role to a colleague on any resource group in that subscription.
opts: True
False
why: Contributor's NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and /Delete, which is exactly what creating a role assignment requires, so a Contributor can manage every resource yet cannot grant anyone access. Only Owner, User Access Administrator, or a custom role that includes the role-assignment write action can do that.

q: When a policy with the Deny effect is assigned at a management group, existing resources beneath it that violate the policy are automatically removed or brought into compliance.
opts: True
False
why: Deny only blocks new create or update requests that would violate the rule. Existing resources are evaluated and reported as non-compliant, but nothing is changed or deleted. Fixing what already exists requires a DeployIfNotExists or Modify policy together with a remediation task.

q: A Global Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID tries to edit a resource group in the Azure portal and gets an access-denied error, despite being a Global Administrator. What lets them manage Azure resources across every subscription in the tenant?
opts: Turning on the "elevate access" setting for Global Administrators in Microsoft Entra ID properties
Assigning themselves the Reader role manually at the tenant root management group scope
Waiting 24 hours for the new Global Administrator role to finish synchronizing to Azure
Creating a brand new subscription under their own account and moving the resource group into it
why: Microsoft Entra roles like Global Administrator control the identity plane, not Azure resources, by default. The "elevate access" setting grants Global Administrators the Azure RBAC User Access Administrator role at the root management group scope, letting them manage resources tenant-wide. Self-assigning just Reader would only grant read access, not the ability to edit; nothing about this permission gap resolves on a timer; and creating a new subscription does nothing for access to resources in existing ones.

q: A finance team's storage account keeps getting accidentally deleted by administrators who legitimately have Contributor access. Which safeguard specifically blocks deletion while still letting their authorized configuration changes continue?
opts: A CanNotDelete resource lock
A ReadOnly resource lock
Revoking Contributor from the whole team
An audit-effect Azure Policy
why: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion but still allows reads and writes. A ReadOnly lock would also block the configuration changes the team needs; removing Contributor access would block those too, and an audit-only policy effect just flags noncompliance without preventing the delete.

q: User1 is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of subscription Sub1 and holds no other role assignments. Which two actions can User1 perform? (Choose two.)
opts: Create a new resource group in Sub1
Deploy a virtual machine into an existing resource group in Sub1
Assign the Reader role to User2 on a resource group in Sub1
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to a resource group in Sub1
why: Contributor grants every action except those under Microsoft.Authorization (role assignments, deny assignments, locks, elevate access) and Blueprints (now being retired in favor of Deployment Stacks), so creating resource groups and deploying resources are both allowed. Assigning a role needs Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which Contributor excludes. The lock is the near-miss: management locks also live under Microsoft.Authorization/locks, so a Contributor can neither create nor remove them, even though it can otherwise fully manage the resource group.

q: Your tenant has 2,000 users. You must block sign-ins that use legacy authentication protocols such as IMAP and SMTP AUTH, but one on-premises scanner account must keep using SMTP AUTH, and users must not be forced to register for MFA as part of this change. What should you configure?
opts: A Conditional Access policy that blocks the Other clients client-app condition, excluding the scanner account
Security defaults enabled at the tenant level in Microsoft Entra ID properties
Per-user multifactor authentication set to Enforced for the user accounts, excluding the scanner
A sign-in risk policy in Microsoft Entra ID Protection that blocks medium and high risk sign-ins
why: Conditional Access exposes legacy protocols as a client-app condition and supports per-user exclusions, so the scanner can be carved out. Security defaults block legacy authentication too, but tenant-wide with no exclusions, and they also require every user to register for MFA. Per-user MFA does not block legacy protocols directly; legacy clients simply fail MFA inconsistently, and it forces registration. A sign-in risk policy reacts to risk signals, not to the protocol a client uses.

q: An organization wants administrators to normally hold no standing Global Administrator access, activating that role with approval and only for a limited, time-boxed window when actually needed. Which feature enables this?
opts: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) with eligible assignments
A quarterly access review of the Global Administrator role
A Conditional Access policy with a one-hour sign-in frequency for administrators
An administrative unit that contains the administrator accounts
why: PIM makes the role assignment eligible rather than active, so the administrator must activate it, optionally with approval and justification, and it expires after the configured duration. An access review is the near-miss: it periodically confirms whether someone should keep a role, but between reviews the assignment is still standing access. A sign-in frequency control forces re-authentication; it does not remove the role between uses. An administrative unit narrows which users a role applies to, not when the role is held.

q: A custom role that grants only Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/restart/action, with no read action, lets the assignee restart virtual machines from the Azure portal.
opts: True
False
why: The portal has to list and open the VM before it can offer a Restart button, and that requires Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read. Without a read action the VM is invisible in the portal, even though a CLI call that targets the resource ID directly could still succeed. Real least-privilege custom roles pair the specific action with the matching read permission.

q: User2 is assigned the Owner role at subscription Sub1. User2 must also be able to reset the passwords of standard, non-administrator users in the Microsoft Entra tenant, and currently receives an access-denied error when trying. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?
opts: Assign User2 the Password Administrator Microsoft Entra role
Assign User2 the Owner role at the Tenant Root Group management group
Assign User2 the User Access Administrator role at the Tenant Root Group
Assign User2 the Global Administrator Microsoft Entra role
why: Password resets are a directory operation, and no Azure RBAC assignment at any scope, even the Tenant Root Group, grants directory permissions; Owner and User Access Administrator there only widen control over Azure resources. Password Administrator is the narrowest Microsoft Entra role that covers resetting passwords for non-administrators. Global Administrator would work but is far broader than the requirement.

q: An organization creates an emergency access ('break-glass') account that's excluded from every Conditional Access policy, in case a misconfigured policy locks out all admins at once. Which additional practice is recommended to keep that account secure?
opts: Give the account a long, complex credential that isn't stored with any one person, plus alerting on any sign-in
Enroll the account in the same Conditional Access policies it was created to bypass, for consistency
Assign the account the Reader role only, so it can never make changes even in a real emergency
Rotate the account's password automatically every 24 hours through a Conditional Access policy
why: A break-glass account needs to stay usable if Conditional Access itself is misconfigured, so it's deliberately excluded from those policies — but it still needs strong secrecy (a long, closely-held credential) and monitoring (alerting on any sign-in, since real use should be rare and noteworthy). Enrolling it back into Conditional Access defeats its purpose, Reader access wouldn't let it actually fix anything during an emergency, and Conditional Access has no role in password rotation.

q: A compliance team wants every new storage account created in a subscription to automatically get a specific diagnostic setting applied at creation time, without anyone remembering to configure it by hand. Which Azure Policy effect fits this?
opts: DeployIfNotExists
Audit
Deny
Append
why: DeployIfNotExists evaluates new or updated resources against a condition and, if it isn't met, automatically deploys a related resource, like a diagnostic setting, to bring the resource into compliance. Audit only flags noncompliant resources in reports without changing them, Deny blocks the resource from being created in the first place rather than fixing it, and Append only adds or overwrites specific fields in the request itself — it doesn't deploy a separate related resource the way this scenario needs.

q: A company has had the same set of guest users with access to a sensitive SharePoint site for two years and wants a recurring, scheduled process where a manager has to explicitly confirm each guest still needs access, or it gets automatically revoked. Which Microsoft Entra feature fits?
opts: An access review of the guest users, recurring quarterly, with results applied automatically
A Conditional Access policy that limits guest sign-in frequency to 24 hours
Privileged Identity Management eligible assignments for the guest users
The guest user access restrictions setting in External collaboration settings
why: Access reviews are the recertification feature: a designated reviewer approves or denies each guest on a schedule and denied users lose access automatically. A sign-in frequency control forces guests to re-authenticate but never asks anyone whether they should still have access. PIM provides time-boxed activation of privileged roles, which does not fit ongoing access to a site. Guest access restrictions limit what guests can see in the directory; they do not review or remove existing site access.

q: If the User Administrator role is assigned to User1 with its scope set to administrative unit AU1, User1 can reset passwords for every non-administrator in the tenant except members of other administrative units.
opts: True
False
why: An administrative-unit-scoped assignment applies only to the users, groups, and devices that are members of that unit. Users who belong to no administrative unit at all are still out of reach. Tenant-wide scope requires assigning the role at the tenant level rather than at AU1.

q: Which two of the following are true about Azure RBAC deny assignments? (Choose two.)
opts: A deny assignment blocks specified actions regardless of any role assignment that would otherwise allow them
Deny assignments are created and managed directly by subscription administrators the same way role assignments are
Deny assignments are most commonly created automatically by deployment stacks or managed apps to protect their own resources
A deny assignment can be overridden by assigning the affected user the Owner role
why: A deny assignment blocks specified actions no matter what role assignments would otherwise allow, and in practice they're usually created automatically by system features like deployment stacks (the successor to Azure Blueprints, which retires on January 31, 2027) and managed applications to protect resources they manage, not hand-authored by administrators the way ordinary role assignments are. Owner access doesn't override a deny assignment — deny always takes precedence over any allow, including Owner.

q: On resource group RG1 you open Access control (IAM) and run Check access for User1. User1 holds Reader on the subscription that contains RG1, Contributor directly on RG1, and Owner on VM1, which is a resource inside RG1. Which assignments does Check access list for User1 at the RG1 scope?
opts: Owner on VM1 only, because Check access reports the single most privileged assignment held anywhere below the scope
Reader, Contributor, and Owner, because Check access always includes assignments made on child scopes below the one you opened
Contributor on RG1 only, because assignments inherited from the subscription are listed only on the subscription's own page
Reader inherited from the subscription, and Contributor on RG1
why: Check access shows the assignments made at the scope and those inherited to it from parents such as the subscription. An assignment made on VM1 is at a child scope, so it is not listed when you look at RG1; open VM1's own IAM page to see it. Inherited assignments are included, which rules out Contributor alone, and the view lists assignments rather than picking the highest-privilege one.

q: Your team has a monthly $5,000 budget on subscription Sub1. When actual cost reaches 100 percent, a Logic App must run that deallocates all VMs tagged Environment=Dev. Which configuration meets the requirement?
opts: An Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect that blocks VM start operations once spend exceeds $5,000
A budget on Sub1 with a 100 percent actual-cost alert that calls an action group running the Logic App
An Azure Advisor cost recommendation configured to run the Logic App when spending passes the threshold
A budget on Sub1 configured with the option to automatically stop and deallocate resources once the amount is reached
why: Budget alerts can call an action group, and an action group can start a Logic App, Automation runbook, or Function, so that is the supported way to react to a breach. A budget by itself only notifies; it has no setting that stops resources. Advisor produces recommendations and does not run actions on cost thresholds. Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and has no visibility of spending.

q: You move VM1, along with its NIC and managed disk, from resource group rg-dev in West Europe to resource group rg-prod, which was created in North Europe. Both are in the same subscription. Which statement describes the result?
opts: The VM stays in West Europe and its resource ID now references rg-prod
The VM is migrated to North Europe and keeps its original resource ID
The VM is stopped and redeployed in North Europe, and gets a new resource ID
The VM keeps its resource ID because only tags and locks are updated
why: Moving a resource changes only its resource group or subscription. The location of the resource does not change, even if the destination group's own location differs, and the resource ID changes because it contains the resource group name. The VM remains operational during the move. Changing the region is a different operation, performed with Azure Resource Mover or Site Recovery.

q: Contoso is changing the Microsoft Entra directory that Sub1 trusts, from the old tenant to a new tenant. After the transfer, an application that runs on a VM in Sub1 with a system-assigned managed identity cannot read secrets, and administrators find that nobody has any Azure role on the subscription. What should you do?
opts: Restore the role assignments by running a reprocess on the subscription in the old directory
Wait for role assignments to replicate from the old directory, which takes up to 24 hours
Re-create the role assignments, custom roles, and managed identities in the target directory
Assign the Global Administrator role in the new tenant, which restores all Azure role assignments
why: When a subscription moves to a different directory, Azure role assignments and custom roles are permanently deleted rather than carried over, and managed identities must be re-created and re-authorized. Nothing replicates later, and the old directory no longer holds the subscription. Global Administrator is a Microsoft Entra role, and it does not recreate Azure RBAC assignments; elevating access is only a way to regain control to make new ones.

q: A policy definition with the deployIfNotExists effect that enables diagnostic settings was assigned to a subscription last year. Forty existing storage accounts are reported non-compliant. Which two statements about fixing them are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A remediation task can deploy the required settings to the existing non-compliant resources
The remediation task uses the managed identity of the policy assignment, which needs sufficient roles on the resources
The standard evaluation cycle remediates existing resources automatically within 24 hours
Changing the effect to Deny remediates existing resources without a task
why: Remediation tasks are how deployIfNotExists and modify policies reach resources that existed before the policy, and the task deploys with the assignment's managed identity, so the identity must hold roles that allow the deployment. The evaluation cycle only recalculates compliance; it does not change existing resources. Deny blocks new or updated resources that violate a rule and never alters existing ones.

q: A group with dynamic user membership assigns Microsoft 365 licenses. A newly created user is a member of the group, but the license shows an error and the user cannot be licensed. The tenant has enough licenses. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The dynamic rule has not been re-evaluated for 24 hours
The user type is Guest, which blocks all licensing
The group is a Microsoft 365 group rather than a security group
The user has no usage location set
why: A license cannot be assigned to a user until a usage location is set, because some services are not available in every country or region. Group-based licensing can use security groups and Microsoft 365 groups, so the group type is not the cause. Guest accounts can be licensed when the product allows it, and the question states that the user is already in the group, so the rule has evaluated.

q: An engineer tries to move VM1 from RG1 to RG2 in the same subscription and the operation fails with an error saying the scope is locked. The VM is running and healthy. Which of the following should you check first?
opts: Whether the VM size supports accelerated networking on its network interface
Whether a read-only lock exists on RG1, RG2, or the subscription
Whether the VM's network security group has an inbound rule allowing port 3389
Whether the VM's operating system disk uses a Premium SSD rather than a Standard SSD
why: A move cannot proceed when a read-only lock exists on the source resource group, the target resource group, or the subscription, because the move writes to those scopes. Running VMs can be moved without being stopped, and NSG rules, disk SKU, and VM size features have no bearing on a scope-locked error.

q: A budget with an alert at 100 percent of actual cost deallocates virtual machines automatically when the amount is reached.
opts: True
False
why: Budgets only generate notifications. To take an action such as deallocating VMs, you attach an action group that triggers automation, such as an Azure Automation runbook or a Logic App. Resources are not affected and spending is not stopped by the budget itself.

q: Assigning a policy with the Deny effect to a subscription removes existing resources that violate the rule.
opts: True
False
why: Deny blocks new and updated resource requests that violate the rule. Resources that already exist are not deleted or changed; they are reported as non-compliant. Bringing them into compliance needs a remediation task for a deployIfNotExists or modify policy, or manual correction.

q: A company needs to grant a third-party app 24-hour, read-only access to a single blob container, without sharing the storage account key.
opts: A Conditional Access policy
The storage account access key
A Shared Access Signature (SAS)
A Read-only resource lock
why: A SAS grants limited, time-boxed, scoped access (read-only, one container, 24 hours) without exposing the account's full access key. Handing over the storage account key would give the app full, unrestricted, non-expiring access to the whole account, far more than needed. A Conditional Access policy governs sign-ins to Microsoft Entra-integrated apps, not access to storage data itself, and a read-only resource lock only prevents accidental deletion/modification of the storage account resource -- it doesn't grant a third party access in the first place.

q: You create a lifecycle management rule on a general-purpose v2 account that moves block blobs to the Cool tier 30 days after they were last accessed. Forty-five days later, blobs that nobody has read since upload are still in the Hot tier. What should you do first?
opts: Enable last access time tracking on the storage account
Change the rule to use days since last modification instead
Change the default access tier of the storage account to Cool
Upgrade the storage account to the Premium performance tier
why: A daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan condition only works once access time tracking is enabled on the account; without it the policy has no last-access timestamp to evaluate and silently skips those blobs. Switching to last-modified would move the blobs but changes the business rule, since a frequently read but rarely modified blob would also be demoted. Changing the default tier affects only new uploads without an explicit tier. Premium block blob accounts do not support Cool or Archive tiers at all.

q: A faulty script overwrote and deleted thousands of blobs in container data1 at 09:14 today. The storage account already has blob versioning, soft delete, change feed, and point-in-time restore enabled. You need to return the entire container to its 09:00 state with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opts: Perform a point-in-time restore of the container to 09:00
Undelete each affected blob and promote its previous version to current
Initiate a customer-managed failover to the secondary region
Copy the container from the most recent blob snapshots with AzCopy
why: Point-in-time restore uses the change feed plus versions and soft-deleted data to roll a whole container, or a range of blobs, back to a chosen moment in one operation. Promoting versions blob by blob reaches the same end state but is thousands of manual actions. A geo-failover does not help because the asynchronous replica already received the destructive writes. Blob snapshots are only created when something explicitly takes them, and nothing in the scenario did.

q: A storage account must stay writable if a single availability zone in its primary region fails, and an application must be able to read its data from the secondary region during a regional outage without waiting for a failover. The solution must minimize cost. Which redundancy option should you choose?
opts: Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) with three copies across zones
why: Surviving a zone loss while staying writable needs synchronous zone redundancy in the primary region, and reading from the secondary before a failover needs the read-access variant, so RA-GZRS is the cheapest option that satisfies both. GZRS covers the zone requirement but the secondary is not readable until you fail over. RA-GRS keeps the secondary readable, but its primary is locally redundant, so a zone failure takes writes offline. ZRS has no secondary region at all.

q: You migrate a departmental file server to Azure. Domain-joined Windows VMs must mount the share, and existing NTFS permissions must keep working so that each user sees only their own folders. The domain is on-premises Active Directory synced to Microsoft Entra ID. What should you deploy?
opts: An Azure Files SMB share with on-premises AD DS authentication enabled
An Azure Files NFS share on a premium file storage account
An Azure Files SMB share mounted with the storage account key
A blob container with the SFTP endpoint enabled
why: Identity-based authentication over SMB lets Azure Files honor Windows ACLs with the users' existing AD DS identities. Mounting with the account key is the near-miss: the share mounts fine, but every user connects as the same super-user identity, so per-user NTFS permissions are not enforced. NFS shares use POSIX permissions and have no Windows Kerberos integration. SFTP on Blob Storage is file transfer, not a mountable share with NTFS semantics.

q: A storage account must accept requests only from two corporate office public IP ranges and from subnet App1 in VNet1. Requests from anywhere else, even with a valid key or SAS, must be refused. What should you configure?
opts: Storage firewall IP rules for the offices plus a virtual network rule for App1
A private endpoint for the storage account in subnet App1 of VNet1
A network security group on the storage account that permits those sources
A SAS token whose allowed IP range is limited to the office addresses
why: The storage firewall is the account-level network control that blocks everything not explicitly allowed, regardless of what credential a caller presents. A private endpoint gives App1 a private path, but on its own it leaves the public endpoint open, and the offices arrive over the internet anyway. NSGs attach to subnets and NICs, not to storage accounts. An IP-restricted SAS only constrains callers using that particular token; the account key and other tokens still work from anywhere.

q: When you create a storage account with geo-redundant storage (GRS), you choose which secondary region the data replicates to.
opts: True
False
why: GRS and GZRS always replicate to the fixed Azure paired region of the primary; the administrator cannot pick a different secondary. If data must be copied to a region of your choosing, that calls for object replication to a second storage account, not a redundancy setting.

q: Enabling soft delete for blobs on a storage account also protects the Azure file shares in that account from accidental deletion.
opts: True
False
why: Blob soft delete and file share soft delete are separate settings configured in different places (Data protection for blobs, the File shares settings for shares) with their own retention periods. Turning on one does nothing for the other, which is a common gap discovered only after a share is deleted.

q: A shared access signature that was signed with storage account key1 keeps working after key1 is regenerated, because the token carries its own expiry time.
opts: True
False
why: A SAS is validated by recomputing its signature with the key that signed it, so regenerating that key immediately invalidates every SAS it signed, whatever their expiry. That is also why rotating keys is the emergency way to revoke an ad hoc SAS, and why a stored access policy is the gentler option for revoking a service SAS without rotating keys.

q: An application's managed identity needs to read and write blobs in a container, without ever handling a SAS token or the storage account key.
opts: Assign the managed identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the container or storage account
Generate a long-lived SAS token and embed it in the application's configuration for the managed identity to use
Share the storage account's access key with the application so it can authenticate directly
Add the application to a dynamic group whose membership rule grants storage access automatically
why: Data-plane RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor let an identity authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID and access blob data directly, with no key or token to manage at all. A SAS token or the account key both reintroduce exactly the credential-handling this scenario wants to avoid, and dynamic groups manage user/group membership rules, not resource-level data permissions.

q: An immutable blob storage policy with a legal hold in effect can be bypassed by the storage account's Owner role to delete data early if needed.
opts: True
False
why: Immutability policies, including legal holds, block deletion and modification for everyone, including the account owner, until the hold is removed or the retention period expires — that is what makes them valid for regulatory retention requirements.

q: A storage account should be reachable from resources inside a specific subnet using the subnet's private IP address space, with traffic never traversing the public internet, and the storage account itself getting an address inside that VNet. Which feature specifically provides this?
opts: A Shared Access Signature
A service endpoint
A storage account firewall IP rule alone
A private endpoint
why: A private endpoint gives the storage account an actual private IP address inside the VNet, so traffic from the subnet stays fully off the public internet. A service endpoint instead extends the subnet's identity over the Microsoft backbone to reach the storage account's still-public endpoint, optimizing the route without the storage account ever getting an address inside the VNet. A SAS only grants a scoped credential, and a firewall IP rule alone still means the storage account is reachable at its public endpoint from allowed IPs, not an address inside your VNet.

q: You create a private endpoint for storage account st1 in VNet1. A VM in VNet1 still resolves st1.blob.core.windows.net to a public IP address, and st1 remains reachable from the internet. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
opts: Link a privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone that holds the endpoint A record to VNet1
Set Public network access on st1 to Disabled
Add a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage to the VM subnet
Add an NSG rule on the VM subnet that allows outbound TCP 443 to the storage service tag
why: The private endpoint only creates a NIC with a private IP; name resolution to that IP depends on a private DNS zone linked to the VNet, and the public endpoint stays open until public network access is disabled or restricted. A service endpoint is the near-miss: it optimizes the route to the public endpoint and does not change DNS or close public access. An NSG rule permitting 443 was never the problem, since traffic to the public endpoint already works.

q: An IoT platform writes about 2 TB of sensor files per day. Files are read often during the first week, rarely afterwards, and must be retained for one year. You need to choose storage that minimizes cost over the retention period. What should you use?
opts: Block blobs in a standard GPv2 account with a lifecycle management policy
Block blobs in a premium block blob storage account for low-latency reads
A standard Azure Files share with daily share snapshots for retention
Azure Table storage with one entity per sensor file and a timestamp property
why: Standard GPv2 blob storage offers Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers, so a lifecycle rule can push each file to cheaper tiers as it ages. Premium block blob accounts give low latency for hot, high-transaction data but offer no cooler tiers, so a year of rarely read files stays at the highest price. Azure Files is priced for file-share semantics and does not tier individual files. Table storage holds structured entities, not multi-megabyte files.

q: A company needs its nightly database export files, currently written to Azure Blob Storage in the Hot tier, to automatically move to the Cool tier after 30 days of no access, and then to the Archive tier after 90 days, without anyone doing it manually. Which feature accomplishes this?
opts: A blob lifecycle management policy with time-based tier transition rules
Changing the storage account's default access tier to Cool
A SAS token scoped to expire after 90 days
Azure Backup configured with a 90-day retention policy
why: Lifecycle management policies automatically transition or delete blobs based on rules like 'no access for N days,' handling exactly this tiering without manual intervention. Changing the account's default tier only affects new blobs uploaded without an explicit tier, a SAS token controls access duration rather than storage tier, and Backup protects against data loss — it doesn't move blobs between access tiers.

q: A branch office runs a local Windows file server that's running low on disk space, but needs to keep offering fast local access to files that are actually opened often. Which Azure service lets infrequently-used files get replaced locally with lightweight pointers to a cloud copy, while frequently-used files stay fully cached on-premises?
opts: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled
AzCopy run on a nightly schedule
A storage account lifecycle management policy
Azure Site Recovery, configured for the file server
why: Azure File Sync keeps an Azure file share and the on-premises file server in sync, and cloud tiering can replace cold, infrequently-accessed files locally with small pointer stubs that fetch the content from Azure on demand, freeing local disk space while keeping hot files cached nearby. AzCopy only performs one-off or scheduled copy jobs, not continuous sync with tiering; a lifecycle policy only moves blobs between access tiers in the cloud, not files on a local server; and Site Recovery replicates whole VMs for disaster recovery, unrelated to local disk space.

q: A media company wants newly uploaded blobs in its primary storage account to be automatically and asynchronously copied to a separate storage account in another region, so read requests from users near that region can be served from a local copy. Which feature fits?
opts: Object replication
Blob lifecycle management
RA-GRS
A storage account access key
why: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs from a source account to a destination account, including across regions, which is exactly this scenario of serving a local copy to users near the second region. Lifecycle management only moves blobs between access tiers within the same account, RA-GRS makes a Microsoft-managed secondary readable but doesn't create an independently addressable second storage account, and an access key is a credential, not a replication mechanism.

q: Customer-initiated storage account failover promotes the secondary region to primary for a GRS account, but data written to the primary just before the outage may not have replicated yet and can be lost.
opts: True
False
why: Because GRS replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, a customer-initiated failover can lose the most recent writes that had not yet replicated — a real tradeoff administrators need to plan around, not a lossless operation.

q: Regulations require that data in storage account st1 is encrypted with a key that your security team controls and rotates, and that the key is held in Azure Key Vault. The account is a general-purpose v2 account that stores blobs and Azure files. Which configuration meets the requirement with the least effort?
opts: Turn on Azure Disk Encryption for the storage account from the Encryption blade in the portal
Enable infrastructure encryption on st1 so that a second layer is applied with a separate key
Have the client application provide its own encryption key on each Blob Storage request
Enable customer-managed keys using a key in a vault with soft delete and purge protection
why: Customer-managed keys are stored in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, rotated by the customer, and apply to Blob Storage and Azure Files. The vault must have soft delete and purge protection. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer but uses Microsoft-managed keys. Customer-provided keys are sent per request and cover only Blob Storage, not files, and they are not held in Key Vault. Azure Disk Encryption is a feature for VM disks, not storage accounts.

q: A storage account was created last month without infrastructure encryption. A new compliance rule demands double encryption for the data it stores. What must you do?
opts: Enable customer-managed keys, which switches on infrastructure encryption as a second layer automatically
Create a new account with infrastructure encryption enabled and copy the data into it
Enable blob versioning, which applies a second encryption layer to every previous version of a blob
Enable infrastructure encryption on the existing account from the Encryption blade in the portal
why: Infrastructure encryption has to be configured when the storage account is created and cannot be enabled afterward, so the data must move to a new account. Customer-managed keys change who controls the service-level key; they do not add a layer. Versioning is a data-protection feature unrelated to encryption layers.

q: Several applications store customer files in one storage account, and the security team wants Customer A's blobs encrypted with a different key from Customer B's blobs, so that Customer A's key can be disabled independently. All files stay in the same account. Which feature should you use?
opts: Immutable storage with a legal hold
Infrastructure encryption
Stored access policies
Encryption scopes
why: An encryption scope applies a separate key, Microsoft-managed or customer-managed, to a container or an individual blob, creating a cryptographic boundary between the customers inside one account. Infrastructure encryption is account-wide and always uses Microsoft-managed keys. Stored access policies control SAS parameters, and legal holds block deletion and changes; neither separates keys.

q: Cloud-only users on Microsoft Entra-joined Windows 11 devices must open an Azure Files SMB share with their Entra credentials. The devices cannot reach any domain controller and the company has no Active Directory. Which identity source should you enable on the storage account?
opts: A shared access signature on the file share
Shared key authentication through the storage account key
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
On-premises Active Directory Domain Services
why: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Entra ID issue Kerberos tickets for cloud-only or hybrid identities, with no need for connectivity to a domain controller. AD DS authentication requires an on-premises domain and clients that can reach its controllers. Account keys and SAS tokens are not identity-based, and they give broad or token-based access instead of per-user permissions.

q: Users of an Azure Files share report that a folder was deleted this morning. The share has daily share snapshots enabled. What is the fastest way to bring the folder back with the least effect on other files?
opts: Open the latest snapshot taken before the deletion and restore the folder from it
Fail over the storage account to its secondary region and copy the folder back from there
Restore the whole storage account from a recovery point held in a Recovery Services vault
Undelete the file share from the list of soft-deleted shares in the storage account
why: Share snapshots are point-in-time copies from which a folder or single file can be restored, so only the deleted content is affected. Soft delete applies when the whole file share is deleted, not a folder inside it. Account failover and a vault restore are heavy tools; the storage account has not failed, and nothing in the question says it is backed up to a vault.

q: Which two statements about Azure Files soft delete and share snapshots are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A share can hold up to 200 snapshots
Share snapshots are full independent copies that are billed for the whole size of the share each time
Soft delete is enabled at the storage account level and covers every share in the account
Soft delete restores a single file that was deleted from within a share
why: Soft delete settings apply per storage account to all shares, and a share supports up to 200 snapshots. Soft delete only protects a deleted share, not individual files inside it; snapshots are for that. Snapshots are incremental, so only changes since the previous snapshot are stored and billed.

q: An administrator holds the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on container c1 only, with no other role on the subscription or storage account. When she signs in to Azure from Storage Explorer, she cannot see the account's containers. What should she do?
opts: Ask for the Owner role on the storage account so that the data role takes effect in the explorer
Attach the container as a single resource and use the Microsoft Entra ID sign-in option
Switch to the storage account key for all future access from her desktop machine
Turn off the storage firewall so that the containers become visible to Storage Explorer
why: After an Azure sign-in, Storage Explorer needs both management-plane and data-plane permissions to enumerate accounts. A person with only a data role can attach to the specific resource using Microsoft Entra ID instead. Owner on the account would grant management access but is far broader than needed. Turning off the firewall and using the account key remove protections and ignore least privilege.

q: You are the Owner of storage account st1 and run azcopy login to copy files into a container. The command fails with an authorization error, although you can see the container in the portal. What is the cause?
opts: AzCopy authenticates only with an account key and cannot use Microsoft Entra ID at all
AzCopy copies only to file shares and does not support blob containers as a destination
The Owner role must be assigned at the subscription scope before AzCopy can use it
Owner does not grant data access; you need a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor
why: Control-plane roles such as Owner do not automatically grant data-plane access. With Microsoft Entra authorization, AzCopy needs an identity with a data role like Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. Alternatively use a SAS token. AzCopy supports Microsoft Entra sign-in, and it works with both blobs and files.

q: You must keep an on-premises folder and a blob container synchronized, so that the container always reflects the folder, including files removed locally. Nothing in the container should ever flow back to the folder. Which command fits?
opts: azcopy copy with --recursive, using the container as the source and the local folder as the destination
azcopy sync from the folder to the container with --delete-destination=true
azcopy login with the --tenant-id switch, which mirrors the folder into the container
azcopy sync with the container as the source and --delete-destination=true set on the command
why: azcopy sync is one-way from the source to the destination, and --delete-destination removes destination files that no longer exist in the source, which gives an exact mirror of the folder. azcopy copy only copies and never removes anything at the destination. Reversing the source and destination would overwrite the local folder from the container. azcopy login only authenticates.

q: The default access tier of a storage account can be set to Archive so that every new blob is stored in the cheapest tier.
opts: True
False
why: The account-level default access tier can only be Hot or Cool. Cold and Archive are set on individual blobs, either directly or through a lifecycle management rule, and an Archive blob is offline until it is rehydrated.

q: A container with 3 million blobs was deleted by mistake yesterday. Blob versioning is enabled and blob soft delete is on, but container soft delete was never configured. Which statement is correct?
opts: Blob soft delete recovers the container together with all of the blobs inside it
It cannot be recovered, because container soft delete is a separate setting that was off
Blob versioning restores the deleted container automatically from the previous version
Share snapshots recover the container, because they were enabled on the account
why: Container soft delete and blob soft delete are configured separately. Blob soft delete protects deleted blobs and snapshots; it does not recover a deleted container, and versions inside a deleted container go with it. Share snapshots are an Azure Files feature and do not apply to blob containers.

q: An administrator wants to change a running VM's managed disk from Standard HDD to Premium SSD to improve performance. What has to happen first?
opts: The VM must be deallocated before the disk tier can be changed
Nothing — the tier can be changed while the VM keeps running
The disk must be deleted and recreated from a snapshot
The VM must be moved to a different region
why: Changing a managed disk's performance tier requires the VM to be stopped (deallocated) first — it isn't a live, no-downtime operation. Deleting and recreating the disk, or moving regions, are unnecessary and far more disruptive than the actual requirement.

q: A stateless web tier must meet a 99.99% availability SLA, and the number of identical VMs must grow and shrink automatically with CPU load. The region supports availability zones. What should you deploy?
opts: A VM Scale Set spread across three availability zones with an autoscale rule
A VM Scale Set in a single zone configured with five fault domains and an autoscale rule
An availability set with two update domains and three fault domains
Three VMs in separate proximity placement groups behind a load balancer
why: The 99.99% VM SLA applies only when instances are spread across two or more availability zones, and a Scale Set is what adds and removes instances automatically. A single-zone Scale Set with fault domains tops out at 99.95%, the same as an availability set, and the availability set cannot autoscale at all. Proximity placement groups pull VMs physically closer together for latency, which is the opposite of spreading risk and carries no SLA uplift.

q: You must run a PowerShell script once on 200 existing Windows VMs to change a registry value. The VMs have no public IP addresses, you must not sign in to any of them, and the change must not be re-applied automatically afterwards. What should you use?
opts: The Custom Script Extension, deployed to each VM
cloud-init configuration added to each VM
Azure Machine Configuration with a configuration package
Scripted Azure Bastion sessions to each VM
why: The Custom Script Extension is delivered through the VM agent, so it runs on existing VMs with no inbound connectivity, executes once, and is done. cloud-init only runs during first boot of a Linux VM, so it cannot touch VMs that already exist. Machine Configuration continuously audits and re-applies desired state, which violates the one-time requirement. Bastion still means an interactive session into each machine.

q: A production App Service app runs in a Standard-tier plan. Each release must be validated against production settings, warmed up, switched to users with no cold start, and reverted within seconds if a problem appears. The solution must minimize cost. What should you do?
opts: Add a staging deployment slot, deploy there, then swap it with production
Create a second App Service plan and shift traffic with weighted Traffic Manager routing
Scale the plan out to two instances and deploy the release to one of them
Move the app to an App Service Environment with a separate staging app
why: Slots run inside the same plan, so there is no extra compute to pay for; the swap warms the staging instance first, then exchanges routing almost instantly, and swapping back is the rollback. A second plan doubles compute cost and DNS-based traffic shifting reverts only as fast as TTLs expire. Instances of one plan all serve the same code, so you cannot deploy to only one of them. An App Service Environment is the most expensive option and solves an isolation problem nobody asked about.

q: A nightly job runs for about 20 minutes inside a Linux container, started by a Logic App. It needs no inbound HTTP endpoint and no scaling to multiple replicas, and you must pay only while it runs. You want to deploy the fewest Azure resources. What should you use?
opts: A container group in Azure Container Instances
An Azure Container Apps app in a new Container Apps environment
Web App for Containers on a Basic App Service plan
An Azure Kubernetes Service cluster with a CronJob
why: A container group is a single resource, bills per second only while the container runs, and the Logic App connector can start and stop it directly. Container Apps is the near-miss: it can also run on-demand work, but it requires a Container Apps environment first and is built around HTTP ingress, revisions, and replica scaling that this job never uses. An App Service plan bills continuously whether or not anything runs. An AKS cluster means node pools and upgrades for a 20-minute job.

q: A company wants microservices-style container scaling with built-in HTTP-based autoscaling, without managing a Kubernetes cluster directly.
opts: Azure Container Apps
An App Service plan alone
Azure Container Instances
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
why: Container Apps adds serverless scaling and microservices features on top of containers, without exposing the underlying cluster.

q: A developer deploys a Bicep file to resource group RG1 using az deployment group create with --mode Complete. Afterwards, a storage account an administrator had created manually in RG1 is gone. Future deployments of the file must update the templated resources without touching anything that is not in the file. What should you do?
opts: Deploy with the Incremental mode instead
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the manually created resources in RG1
Run the what-if operation before each deployment
Declare the storage account in the Bicep file so Complete mode keeps it
why: Complete mode deletes any resource in the group that the template does not declare; Incremental, the default, leaves undeclared resources alone and still updates the ones that are declared. A lock would make the Complete-mode deployment fail when it tries to delete the locked resource rather than make the deployment safe. What-if previews the deletions but does nothing to prevent them. Adding the storage account to the file works for that one resource, but it means every hand-made resource must be maintained in the template forever.

q: VM1, VM2, and VM3 are in availability set AS1. You deallocate VM1 and try to resize it to Standard_E8s_v5, but that size is not offered for VM1 even though other VMs in the region can use it. You need to complete the resize with the least disruption. What should you do?
opts: Deallocate all three VMs in AS1, resize VM1, then start them
Remove VM1 from AS1, resize it, then add it back to AS1
Delete VM1 and recreate it from its disks in a new availability set
Move VM1 to a different resource group and resize it there
why: VMs in an availability set are pinned to a shared hardware cluster, so a size that cluster lacks only becomes available once every VM in the set is deallocated and the set can be placed on a cluster that offers it. A VM cannot be moved into or out of an availability set after creation, so removing VM1 from AS1 and adding it back is not possible. Recreating the VM is far more disruptive than a coordinated stop. Resource group membership has no effect on which hardware cluster hosts the VM.

q: A SQL Server VM needs a 512 GiB data disk that delivers 20,000 IOPS, and you must be able to raise or lower the IOPS later without resizing the disk or redeploying the VM. The VM size and region support every disk type. The solution must minimize cost. Which disk type should you use?
opts: Premium SSD v2
Ultra Disk
Premium SSD (P20) with on-demand bursting enabled
Standard SSD (E20)
why: Premium SSD v2 decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity, so 20,000 IOPS can be provisioned on 512 GiB and adjusted later, at a lower price than Ultra Disk. Ultra Disk meets every technical requirement but costs more for the same numbers. A P20 delivers 2,300 baseline IOPS, and on-demand bursting is only offered on disks larger than 512 GiB, so it cannot be enabled here. Standard SSD E20 provides 500 IOPS.

q: An autoscale rule on a VM Scale Set can use a metric from a different resource, such as the active message count of a Service Bus queue, instead of a metric emitted by the scale set itself.
opts: True
False
why: Autoscale rules let you pick a different metric source resource, so a worker tier can scale on queue depth, storage queue length, or any other Azure Monitor metric rather than only on its own CPU or memory. The common misconception is that scale sets can only react to host metrics from their own instances.

q: Deploying the same Bicep file a second time to the same resource group fails because the resources it declares already exist.
opts: True
False
why: Resource Manager deployments are idempotent: a resource that already matches the template is left as is, and one whose properties differ is updated in place. Repeating a deployment is the normal way to roll out changes. The only time a redeploy removes anything is Complete mode, which deletes resources that are missing from the file.

q: An Azure Container Instances container group can run several containers that share the same host, lifecycle, local network, and mounted volumes.
opts: True
False
why: A container group is scheduled as a unit, much like a Kubernetes pod: its containers start and stop together, reach each other on localhost, and can mount the same Azure Files volume. What Container Instances lacks is orchestration across many groups, such as replica scaling and rolling updates, which is where Container Apps or AKS come in.

q: A batch rendering job can tolerate being interrupted and restarted, and the team wants to run it on Azure VMs at a steep discount versus pay-as-you-go pricing.
opts: Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Reserved Instances
A VM Scale Set with manual scaling
Azure Dedicated Host
why: Spot VMs use Azure's unused capacity at a steep discount but can be evicted with little notice when that capacity is needed back — a good fit for interruptible workloads. Reserved Instances are a billing commitment for guaranteed capacity, not an eviction-prone discount.

q: You plan to attach Premium SSD v2 disks to a new virtual machine. Which two statements about Premium SSD v2 are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It cannot be used as the operating system disk of the VM
Its IOPS and throughput can be adjusted without changing the disk size
It supports ReadOnly host caching on the VM
It requires the VM to be deployed in a proximity placement group
why: Premium SSD v2 is a data-disk-only type, and its headline feature is performance provisioned independently of capacity, the same decoupling Ultra Disk offers at a lower price. Host caching is the near-miss: the original Premium SSD supports ReadOnly and ReadWrite caching, but Premium SSD v2 does not, which matters when migrating a disk that relied on it. Proximity placement groups are unrelated to disk type.

q: An administrator deploys three VMs into the same availability zone within a region for a critical app. What risk does this configuration still leave unaddressed, compared to spreading them across three separate zones?
opts: A failure affecting that one physical datacenter
A single VM crashing due to an application bug
A DDoS attack against the application
An expired SSL certificate on the app
why: Placing all three VMs in the same availability zone means they all still depend on that one physical datacenter — a power or cooling failure there could take out all three simultaneously, which is exactly the risk spreading them across zones addresses. The other three risks, an application bug, a DDoS attack, and an expired certificate, are not related to physical datacenter placement at all, so zone distribution would not change any of them.

q: An organization wants to build one standardized, versioned custom VM image and make it available for deployment across multiple subscriptions and regions in their tenant. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Compute Gallery with an image definition and versions replicated to each region
A managed disk snapshot copied to a storage account in each target region
The Custom Script Extension with the configuration applied at first boot
A managed image created in each region from a generalized copy of the VM
why: Azure Compute Gallery is built for publishing versioned images, replicating them to chosen regions, and sharing them across subscriptions or the whole tenant. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of one disk with no versioning or sharing model. The Custom Script Extension configures a VM after it is already running rather than producing an image. A managed image is the near-miss: it is a real image, but it is regional, unversioned, and lives in one subscription, so you would end up maintaining many copies by hand.

q: Applying Azure Hybrid Benefit to a Windows Server VM eliminates the compute charge for that VM entirely, leaving only a licensing fee.
opts: True
False
why: Azure Hybrid Benefit only offsets the licensing portion of the cost by letting you reuse an eligible on-premises license — it does not eliminate the underlying compute charge for the VM's CPU, memory, and disk, which is billed separately regardless of licensing.

q: You migrate a line-of-business application to Azure. Its installer registers a Windows service, writes under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, and loads a third-party kernel-mode driver. You want the lowest operational overhead that still supports the application. Where should you host it?
opts: An Azure virtual machine
Azure App Service on a Windows plan
Azure Container Apps with a Windows container image
Azure Functions on a Premium plan
why: Installing services and kernel drivers requires full control of the guest operating system, which only a VM provides. The App Service sandbox blocks Windows services, kernel drivers, and HKLM writes. Container Apps runs Linux containers only, and a kernel driver cannot be packaged into a container in any case. Functions hosts event-driven code, not an installer-based desktop application.

q: A team runs a VM Scale Set where new instances need a configuration script to run automatically the moment they're provisioned, with no one logging in manually. They also want existing instances to keep running with their current configuration even after the script is updated later. Which approach fits both requirements?
opts: Add the Custom Script Extension to the Scale Set model, so it runs on each new instance without touching existing ones
Run the script manually on each new instance as it appears, using the Run Command feature in the portal
Add the script to a scheduled task on each instance that re-runs whenever the Scale Set model is updated
Use Azure Machine Configuration to apply the script to the existing and new instances nightly
why: Adding the Custom Script Extension to the Scale Set model makes it part of every new instance's provisioning, but with a Manual upgrade policy an updated model is not pushed to instances that already exist, which matches both requirements. Run Command on each new instance reintroduces the human step the team wants removed. A scheduled task keyed to model updates and Machine Configuration both force the change onto existing instances, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid.

q: A latency-sensitive trading application splits its workload across three VMs that constantly exchange data with each other, and the team wants Azure to place them as physically close together as possible within a datacenter to minimize network latency between them. Which feature fits?
opts: A proximity placement group
An availability set
An availability zone
A VM Scale Set
why: A proximity placement group is specifically for colocating VMs physically close together to minimize inter-VM network latency. An availability set and availability zones do the opposite, deliberately spreading VMs apart across hardware or datacenters for resiliency, and a Scale Set manages a group of identical instances but doesn't by itself guarantee physical proximity between them.

q: A team updates their VM Scale Set's model with a new image version and wants Azure to update instances automatically in small batches, pausing to confirm each batch is healthy before moving to the next, rather than updating everything at once or requiring someone to upgrade each instance by hand. Which upgrade policy fits?
opts: Rolling
Manual
Automatic
Spot
why: A Rolling upgrade policy updates instances in batches with health checks between batches, limiting the damage if a bad update slips through. Manual requires explicitly triggering the upgrade on each instance, Automatic updates every instance right away with no batching or health gating, and Spot isn't an upgrade policy at all — it's a VM pricing and eviction model.

q: An administrator wants to capture a configured VM as a reusable image that deploys new VMs with fresh, unique identities, not clones carrying the original VM's exact hostname and security identifiers. What must happen to the source VM immediately before capturing the image?
opts: Generalize it with Sysprep on Windows or waagent -deprovision on Linux
Deallocate it and take an incremental snapshot of the OS disk first
Enable boot diagnostics and reset the local administrator password
Add it to a proximity placement group and resize it to the smallest size
why: Generalizing strips machine-specific state such as the hostname, security identifiers, and cached credentials, so an image built from it produces clean, unique VMs on each deployment. A snapshot is the near-miss: it captures the disk faithfully, but a VM created from a specialized snapshot is an exact clone with the same SID and name. Boot diagnostics, password resets, placement groups, and resizing change nothing about the identity baked into the disk.

q: Enabling encryption at host for a virtual machine requires installing the Azure Disk Encryption extension inside the guest operating system.
opts: True
False
why: Encryption at host is a platform setting on the VM that encrypts temp disks and disk caches on the host itself, with no agent or extension in the guest. Azure Disk Encryption is the separate in-guest option that uses BitLocker or DM-Crypt, and the two cannot be enabled on the same VM, so confusing them leads to a failed configuration rather than extra protection.

q: You have an ARM template and must deploy it to resource group RG1 in Complete mode. Before the deployment, the change approver must see exactly which existing resources would be deleted and which would be modified, without changing anything. What should you run?
opts: az group export, which lists resources that are not in the template
az deployment group validate, which lists every resource it would delete
az bicep build, which compares the template with the live resources
az deployment group what-if with the template and Complete mode
why: The what-if operation compares the template with the current state and reports Create, Modify, Delete, and other change types without deploying, and it respects the deployment mode. Validate only checks that the template and parameters are valid and the deployment could start; it does not list changes. Bicep build compiles Bicep to JSON and has no live comparison. Export generates a new template from live resources rather than a diff.

q: Two years ago an engineer deployed a template that created RG-Web. Since then, administrators have changed several settings by hand in the portal. You need a template that reflects the resources exactly as they are today, and you also need to select only some of the resources. What should you do?
opts: Run az bicep decompile against the original template file
Export the template from the resource group, selecting the required resources
Save the template from the deployment history of the original deployment
Deploy the original template in Incremental mode to read its current values
why: Exporting from a resource group or resource produces a snapshot of the current state, includes manual changes, and lets you choose which resources to include. Saving from history returns the exact original template, so later manual changes are missing and you cannot pick a subset. Decompile only converts a template's syntax and has no knowledge of the live environment. A deployment changes the environment instead of reading it.

q: A team has a library of ARM JSON templates and wants to adopt Bicep. You need to convert main.json to a Bicep file, accepting that the result may need manual cleanup. Which command should you use?
opts: az bicep decompile --file main.json
az bicep build --file main.json
az deployment group export --name main
az bicep upgrade --file main.json
why: az bicep decompile turns an ARM template into main.bicep, on a best-effort basis that can produce warnings to fix by hand. az bicep build goes the other way, compiling Bicep into JSON. Exporting a deployment retrieves a template and does not convert it, and az bicep upgrade updates the Bicep tooling to the latest version rather than converting any file.

q: A template exported from a resource group is guaranteed to deploy unchanged in another subscription, because the export includes every parameter and all dependencies.
opts: True
False
why: Export is not guaranteed to succeed, and the generated template is a snapshot with mostly hard-coded values and often missing parameters, such as some password parameters. It usually needs cleanup before reuse. A template saved from deployment history is the cleaner, parameterized copy.

q: A Bicep file contains the following resource declaration: resource st 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-05-01' = [for i in range(0, 3): { name: 'st${i}${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}', location: resourceGroup().location, sku: { name: 'Standard_LRS' }, kind: 'StorageV2' }]. What does a successful deployment of this file to RG1 create?
opts: Three storage accounts, with names starting st0, st1, and st2
No storage accounts, because the loop only defines a variable
Three storage accounts, with names starting st1, st2, and st3
One storage account whose name contains a list of three suffixes
why: range(0, 3) yields 0, 1, and 2, so the for expression creates three resources, and the index is part of each name. Names that start at 1 confuse range with a one-based count. A for expression around a resource declaration deploys one resource per element rather than a single one, and it is a resource loop, not a variable declaration.

q: VM security policy requires that temporary disks and disk caches on new VMs are encrypted at rest and that data flows to storage encrypted, using customer-managed keys. No agent may be installed in the guest operating system. Which solution meets the requirement?
opts: Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys, which is on by default
Azure Disk Encryption with BitLocker for Windows and DM-Crypt for Linux
Storage account infrastructure encryption on the account holding the disks
Encryption at host with a disk encryption set that uses customer-managed keys
why: Encryption at host is performed by the host, covers temp disks and caches, encrypts data flowing to storage, supports customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set, and needs nothing inside the guest. Azure Disk Encryption works inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt, so it needs a VM extension, and it cannot be combined with encryption at host. Default platform-managed server-side encryption leaves the temp disk and cache uncovered. Infrastructure encryption is a storage account feature, and managed disks are not governed by it.

q: You registered the EncryptionAtHost feature for the subscription. VM1 is running and has data on a managed disk. You must turn on encryption at host for VM1. What should you do?
opts: Detach all data disks, enable the setting, and then reattach them
Deallocate VM1, enable encryption at host, and start VM1 again
Install the Azure Disk Encryption extension first, then enable the setting
Enable the setting while VM1 is running; it applies at the next hourly sync
why: Encryption at host is enabled on an existing VM only when the VM is deallocated, then it takes effect when the VM starts again. It is not applied to a running VM, it cannot coexist with Azure Disk Encryption, and the data disks do not need to be detached.

q: VM1, its virtual network, NIC, and managed disks are in West Europe. You must move them to North Europe. You want dependencies validated automatically, an option to test the move and discard it, and cleanup of the source after the move. Which service should you use?
opts: Azure Backup with a restore to a new VM in the same vault region
The Move resources option to another resource group
A resource lock on VM1 followed by a subscription transfer
Azure Resource Mover
why: Azure Resource Mover moves VMs and associated resources between regions, resolves dependencies, lets you commit or discard, and can delete the source afterward. Moving to another resource group or subscription changes only the container and leaves the region as it was. A restore into the same vault region does not relocate the workload, and locks and subscription transfers have nothing to do with regions.

q: A container app processes web requests. It must scale out when an average of more than 50 concurrent HTTP requests per replica occur, and it must use no compute charges when it receives no traffic for a while. Which configuration meets the requirement?
opts: A custom CPU rule set to 50 percent and a minimum of 2 replicas
A manual replica count of 50 on the container app environment
An HTTP scale rule with a concurrent request threshold of 50 and a minimum of 0 replicas
A TCP scale rule set to 50 connections and a minimum of 1 replica
why: An HTTP scale rule scales on concurrent requests, and a minimum of zero lets the app scale to zero so that no usage charges accrue when idle. A TCP rule counts connections, not requests, and holding one replica always running keeps charges flowing. A CPU rule measures utilization and a minimum of two keeps instances warm all the time. A fixed manual count has no rule and never scales in.
