q: Users of a container app complain about a long delay on the first request after a quiet night. The app uses an HTTP scale rule and the default replica limits. You must remove the delay while keeping autoscaling. What should you change?
opts: Increase the maximum number of replicas to 1,000
Move the app to Azure Container Instances
Replace the HTTP rule with a TCP rule
Set the minimum number of replicas to 1
why: The default minimum is 0, so the app scales to zero when idle and the first request waits for a replica to start. Setting a minimum of 1 or higher keeps a replica running while the rules continue to add more. A higher maximum only changes the ceiling. A TCP rule scales to zero in the same way, and Container Instances has no autoscaling at all.

q: A container runs a data conversion once, then exits with code 0 when finished. If the process fails, it should be retried automatically. You do not want the container group to be started again after a successful run, so that billing stops. Which restart policy should you set for the Azure Container Instances group?
opts: Always, with an Automation runbook to stop it
OnFailure
Always
Never, because Never retries failures
why: OnFailure restarts the containers only if the process ends with a nonzero exit code and lets a successful run stop for good, which ends billing. Always restarts even after a successful exit, which means the group runs forever. Never does not restart after a successful exit, but it is not designed as the retry-on-failure policy the question needs. A runbook to stop an Always group is unnecessary complexity.

q: Operations wants the container images in a private Azure Container Registry rebuilt automatically whenever the Microsoft-published base image they use is updated, without a separate build server. Which should you use?
opts: A GitHub Actions secret that stores the admin password
A webhook that deletes old tags nightly
Geo-replication on a Premium registry
ACR Tasks with a base image update trigger
why: ACR Tasks builds images in the cloud and can be triggered by a base image update, a source commit, or a timer, so images are rebuilt and patched automatically. Geo-replication copies registries across regions and does not build anything. Storing the admin password is an authentication choice and not a trigger. Deleting old tags tidies the registry rather than rebuilding images.

q: You must map the root domain contoso.com, not a subdomain, to an App Service app and verify domain ownership. Which DNS records should you create?
opts: An MX record pointing to the app's default hostname and an NS record delegating the zone
Two CNAME records, one for contoso.com and one for www.contoso.com, both pointing to the app
An A record to the app's IP address and a TXT record named asuid with the verification ID
A CNAME record to the app's default hostname, plus a TXT record named asuid for verification
why: A root (apex) domain maps with an A record to the app's IP address, and the asuid TXT record carries the custom domain verification ID that proves ownership and prevents subdomain takeover. A CNAME cannot be used at the root of a domain, and MX and NS records have nothing to do with directing web traffic to an app.

q: An app at www.contoso.com and its sibling apps need HTTPS for *.contoso.com with a single wildcard certificate that already exists in Azure Key Vault. The apps run in a Standard App Service plan. Which approach should you use?
opts: Import the certificate from Key Vault into App Service and create SNI SSL bindings
Upload the certificate as a public certificate and bind it to the domain
Scale the plan down to Shared so wildcard certificates are supported
Create a free App Service managed certificate for the wildcard name
why: An existing private certificate, including a wildcard, can be imported from Key Vault and bound with SNI SSL. The free managed certificate does not support wildcards. Public certificates are not used to secure custom domains. Certificates require a Basic or higher plan, so the Shared tier would remove support instead of adding it.

q: A web app runs in the Shared (D1) pricing tier of an App Service plan. You attempt to add a custom domain TLS binding with a purchased certificate and the option is unavailable. What should you do?
opts: Create a deployment slot and bind the certificate there
Enable HTTPS Only in the app's settings
Scale the App Service plan up to the Basic tier or higher
Scale the plan out to two instances
why: Certificates and TLS bindings need a Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated plan, so the plan must be scaled up. Adding instances does not change the tier, slots also depend on higher tiers, and HTTPS Only just redirects traffic and does not provide a certificate.

q: Policy requires App Service app backups kept for 90 days that can be downloaded and archived by the security team. The app is in a Standard plan. Which approach meets the requirement?
opts: Swap the production slot with a staging slot each week to act as a point-in-time backup
Configure custom backups to a storage account with long retention and download them
Rely on automatic backups, which keep 90 days of history when the plan is Standard
Configure automatic backups in the portal with a 90-day retention period
why: Custom backups write to a storage account you choose, can be kept from 0 to 30 days or indefinitely, and can be downloaded as blobs. Automatic backups are fixed at 30 days of retention, cannot be configured, and cannot be downloaded. A slot swap exchanges content between slots and is not a backup.

q: An engineer restores a backup over the production app during business hours and users see an outage while it runs. For future restores, what should you recommend to minimize downtime?
opts: Scale the plan out before restoring so that other instances keep serving users
Restore only the content, because the configuration restore causes the outage
Stop the app, restore, then start it, because that is faster
Restore the backup to a deployment slot, validate it, and swap it into production
why: App Service stops the target app while a restore is running. Restoring into a staging slot and swapping avoids any downtime for the production slot. Extra instances do not help because the target app is stopped as a whole, and stopping the app manually does not shorten the work.

q: An App Service app must call an Azure SQL Managed Instance by its private IP address inside VNet1, and it must be reachable by clients only through the private network. Which two features should you configure? (Choose two.)
opts: Regional virtual network integration for outbound calls
Hybrid connections for traffic to the managed instance
A private endpoint on the web app for inbound access
A service tag on the app's public hostname
why: Virtual network integration provides the outbound path from the app into the VNet, and a private endpoint provides private inbound access, because integration alone never makes an app reachable privately. A service tag is a label used in network rules and does not grant connectivity. Hybrid connections relay traffic to specific endpoints, usually on-premises, and are not needed for a managed instance reachable inside the VNet.

q: Enabling regional virtual network integration for an App Service app lets clients in the virtual network reach the app on a private IP address.
opts: True
False
why: Virtual network integration is for outbound calls from the app into the virtual network only. Private inbound access needs a private endpoint, or an App Service Environment for the entire environment.

q: An app must accept requests only from the subnet that holds an Application Gateway, and all other callers must be rejected at the App Service front end. Which feature meets the requirement?
opts: A deployment slot configured with the public IP address of the Application Gateway
An access restriction that allows the gateway subnet using a service endpoint
An NSG on the Application Gateway subnet that denies all outbound traffic to the internet
Virtual network integration into the Application Gateway subnet for the web app
why: Access restrictions are inbound allow and deny rules enforced by the App Service front ends, and they can match a subnet through a service endpoint. An NSG on the gateway subnet does not govern what the app accepts, virtual network integration is outbound only, and a slot is a deployment construct rather than a filter.

q: A production web app is in a Basic-tier App Service plan. The team wants traffic-driven autoscale rules and a staging slot with swap. What is the minimum change that enables both?
opts: Move the app to the Free tier and enable preview features
Scale out the plan to three instances
Create a second App Service plan in Basic and use Traffic Manager
Scale up the plan to the Standard tier
why: Autoscale and deployment slots begin at the Standard tier, while Basic supports only manual scale-out and has no slots. Adding instances changes the instance count and not the feature set. Free has fewer features than Basic. A second Basic plan with Traffic Manager adds cost and does not provide slots or autoscale.

q: Two NSG rules apply to the same NIC: one at priority 100 allowing inbound port 443, another at priority 200 denying all inbound traffic. What happens to inbound HTTPS traffic?
opts: Both rules apply, and the NIC merges them into a partial allow
It's denied, since a Deny rule takes precedence over an Allow rule whenever both target the same traffic
It's allowed, since the lower priority number is processed first
It's denied, since NSG rules are evaluated from the highest priority number down to the lowest
why: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first and win — priority 100 (allow) is processed before priority 200 (deny), so the traffic is allowed. Deny doesn't have some inherent precedence over Allow, evaluation order runs from the lowest priority number up (not the other way around), and NSG rules aren't merged or blended — whichever rule is evaluated first decides the outcome outright.

q: Hub-VNet contains an Azure Firewall. Spoke1 and Spoke2 are each peered with Hub-VNet. Traffic between Spoke1 and Spoke2 must pass through the firewall for inspection, and you must not create any additional peerings. What should you configure?
opts: Route tables on the spoke subnets sending the other spoke's prefix to the firewall's private IP as next hop
Use remote gateways on the spoke peerings and Allow gateway transit on the hub side of each peering
Allow forwarded traffic on the existing hub and spoke peerings, with no other changes
A direct peering between Spoke1 and Spoke2 with the hub firewall configured as its gateway
why: Peering is not transitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic only flows if a user-defined route sends it to the firewall as a virtual appliance next hop. Gateway transit is the near-miss: it shares a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway through the hub, not a firewall or NVA. Allow forwarded traffic is required for the firewall's forwarded packets to be accepted, but on its own nothing routes to the firewall in the first place. A direct spoke-to-spoke peering violates the constraint and bypasses inspection.

q: A web application runs in App Service in East US and West Europe. Users worldwide must be routed to the nearest healthy region, requests to /api and /images must go to different backend pools, a web application firewall must inspect traffic, and TLS must terminate at the edge. Which service should you deploy?
opts: Azure Front Door Premium
Application Gateway v2 with the WAF SKU
Traffic Manager with the Performance routing method
A cross-region Azure Load Balancer
why: Front Door is the global layer-7 entry point: it chooses the closest healthy origin, routes by URL path, includes WAF, and terminates TLS at Microsoft's edge. Application Gateway offers the same path routing and WAF but is regional, so it would need a global service in front of it to steer users between regions. Traffic Manager steers by DNS and never sees the HTTP request, so no path routing, WAF, or TLS termination. Cross-region Load Balancer works at layer 4.

q: Two network virtual appliances in an active-active pair must receive every TCP and UDP flow from the spoke subnets, on any port, through a single internal load balancer frontend. What should you create?
opts: A Standard internal load balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule
A Basic internal load balancer with one load-balancing rule per protocol and port
An Application Gateway v2 with both appliances in its backend pool
A Standard public load balancer with an outbound rule for the spoke subnets
why: An HA ports rule (port 0, protocol All) on a Standard internal load balancer forwards every port and protocol to the backend pool, which is exactly the pattern for highly available NVAs. The Basic SKU has no HA ports feature, and one rule per port cannot cover every port anyway. Application Gateway only handles HTTP and HTTPS. An outbound rule provides SNAT for egress; it does not distribute inbound flows to the appliances. The Basic SKU was also retired on September 30, 2025.

q: VMs in VNet1 must resolve each other by name under corp.internal, with records created and removed automatically as VMs are deployed and deleted. VMs in VNet2 must resolve those same names, but VNet2's own VMs must not register records. What should you do?
opts: A private DNS zone corp.internal linked to VNet1 with auto-registration on and to VNet2 with auto-registration off
A private DNS zone corp.internal linked to both VNets with auto-registration enabled on both links
A public Azure DNS zone corp.internal with name servers delegated from both virtual networks
Custom DNS servers on VNet2 set to the private IP addresses of two VMs in VNet1
why: Auto-registration is a per-link setting on a private DNS zone, so you can register from VNet1 while VNet2 gets resolution only. Enabling it on both links would make VNet2's VMs register records too. A public zone would expose the names on the internet and cannot auto-register VMs. Pointing VNet2 at VMs in VNet1 presumes those VMs run a DNS service and recreates by hand what a private zone link does natively.

q: Azure Bastion (Basic SKU) is deployed in VNet1. Administrators must connect to VMs in VNet1 using the native ssh client and key files on their workstations rather than the browser, and the VMs must still have no public IP addresses. What should you do?
opts: Upgrade the Bastion host to the Standard SKU and enable native client support
Deploy an additional Bastion host in each subnet that contains VMs
Assign a public IP to each VM and allow TCP 22 from the administrators' addresses in the NSG
Enable just-in-time VM access in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
why: Native client connectivity through az network bastion ssh or tunnel is a Standard-SKU feature; the Basic SKU is browser-only. One Bastion host serves a whole VNet, and even peered VNets, so more hosts add cost without adding the feature. Public IPs break the stated constraint. Just-in-time access narrows when an NSG rule is open, but it still needs the VM to be reachable through a public IP or a VPN.

q: VM1 in subnet A cannot reach VM2 in subnet B on TCP 1433. Both subnets are in the same VNet, and a route table is associated with subnet A. You suspect the traffic is being sent to a network virtual appliance that is offline. Which Network Watcher tool shows where VM1's packets to VM2 are being sent?
opts: Next hop
IP flow verify
Effective security rules
NSG flow logs
why: Next hop evaluates the effective routes for a source VM and destination address and reports the next hop type and IP, which exposes a user-defined route pointing at a dead appliance. IP flow verify is the near-miss: it answers only whether an NSG rule allows or denies the flow, and says nothing about routing. Effective security rules lists the NSG rules applied to a NIC, and flow logs record what the NSGs allowed or denied after the fact.

q: You are adding a subnet to VNet1 (10.10.0.0/16) that must host 60 virtual machines, each with a single network interface, and you want to consume as little address space as possible. Which subnet prefix should you use?
why: Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet (network, broadcast, and three for the platform), so a /26 provides 64 minus 5, or 59 usable addresses, one short of the 60 NICs. A /25 yields 123 usable and is the smallest prefix that fits. A /27 leaves 27. A /24 works but wastes space, and 10.10.0.0/24 may collide with an existing subnet at the start of the range.

q: Application-tier VMs in VNet1 are spread across three availability zones and listen on TCP 8443 and a custom UDP port. Web-tier VMs in peered VNet2 must reach them through one private IP address that keeps working if a zone fails. Nothing may be exposed to the internet. What should you deploy?
opts: A Standard internal load balancer with a zone-redundant frontend
A Basic internal load balancer with a frontend in the application subnet
A Standard public load balancer with an NSG that denies the Internet service tag
An Application Gateway v2 with a private frontend IP address
why: Only the Standard SKU supports availability zones, and a zone-redundant frontend is served from every zone so the single private IP survives a zone outage. The Basic SKU is the near-miss: it is internal and private, but it has no zone awareness and goes down with its zone. A public load balancer wrapped in an NSG still has an internet-facing IP. Application Gateway proxies HTTP and HTTPS only, so the UDP port rules it out. The Basic SKU was also retired on September 30, 2025.

q: Two virtual networks whose address spaces overlap can be peered as long as the overlapping ranges are not assigned to any subnet.
opts: True
False
why: Peering is refused whenever the address spaces overlap at all, used or not, because Azure routes between peered networks by address space, not by subnet. Fixing it means removing the overlapping prefix from one VNet's address space before the peering can be created.

q: A network security group associated with a subnet also filters traffic between two virtual machines that are both inside that same subnet.
opts: True
False
why: A subnet-level NSG is enforced on every flow to and from the NICs in that subnet, including VM-to-VM traffic that never leaves it. The default AllowVnetInBound rule is why that traffic normally works, and a custom deny rule with a lower priority number will block it, which surprises people who assume the NSG only guards the subnet boundary.

q: You plan to deploy Azure Bastion (Standard SKU) into VNet1 (10.1.0.0/16) so administrators can reach VMs that have no public IP addresses. Which subnet should you create for the Bastion host?
opts: AzureBastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
AzureBastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/27
BastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
GatewaySubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
why: The subnet name must be exactly AzureBastionSubnet, and it must be /26 or larger so the service can scale its instances. A /27 is rejected at deployment time. A differently named subnet is simply not recognized by Bastion. GatewaySubnet is the reserved name for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, which cannot be shared with Bastion.

q: An administrator wants one NSG rule that allows traffic to every VM tagged as 'WebTier,' regardless of each VM's individual IP address, which changes as instances are added or removed.
opts: Group the VMs’ network interfaces into an Application Security Group and reference it in the rule
Write a separate NSG rule for every VM's current IP address, updating it manually each time an instance changes
Replace the NSG with a public Load Balancer configured with the same allow rule
Move all the VMs into one dedicated subnet and apply the rule to that subnet as a whole
why: An Application Security Group (ASG) groups VM network interfaces logically, like 'WebTier,' so an NSG rule can reference the group as a source or destination instead of hardcoding IP addresses that change over time. Per-IP rules break the moment an instance is replaced, a Load Balancer distributes traffic but doesn't filter it the way an NSG rule does, and a subnet-wide rule would also catch any other VM later placed in that same subnet.

q: Virtual network flow logs, viewed through Traffic Analytics, can show which allowed and denied flows are hitting resources in a virtual network without manually correlating raw log files. They replace NSG flow logs, which retire on September 30, 2027.
opts: True
False
why: Network Watcher flow logs record IP traffic, and Traffic Analytics processes them in a Log Analytics workspace into visual, queryable insights instead of raw JSON. NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027 and can no longer be created, so virtual network flow logs, enabled at the virtual network, are the current feature.

q: An administrator wants traffic from a subnet destined for the internet to be forced through a network virtual appliance for inspection first, instead of going directly out. Which feature enables this custom routing?
opts: A user-defined route in a route table with the appliance as the next hop
A network security group rule that redirects outbound traffic to the appliance
VNet peering between the subnet's VNet and the appliance's VNet with gateway transit
A NAT gateway associated with the subnet in front of the appliance
why: A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop type Virtual appliance overrides the default internet system route, so the subnet's egress is steered through the appliance. NSG rules allow or deny traffic; they have no concept of redirecting it. Peering with gateway transit shares a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, not an inspection appliance, and establishes connectivity rather than a forced path. A NAT gateway performs outbound SNAT for the subnet and would send traffic straight to the internet, bypassing the appliance.

q: A subnet with several VMs needs reliable outbound-only internet connectivity that does not consume a public IP on each individual VM, and avoids SNAT port exhaustion under heavy outbound load. Which service fits best?
opts: A public Load Balancer
Azure Bastion
A NAT gateway
A private endpoint
why: A NAT gateway provides scalable, outbound-only internet connectivity for an entire subnet through a small pool of shared public IPs, specifically designed to avoid the SNAT port exhaustion a Load Balancer's outbound rules can run into under heavy load. Azure Bastion is for inbound RDP or SSH management access, not outbound internet traffic, and a private endpoint is for inbound access to a specific PaaS resource, not outbound internet connectivity at all.

q: An application in two regions sits behind an Azure Traffic Manager profile. Which two statements describe how Traffic Manager behaves? (Choose two.)
opts: It returns a DNS response pointing the client at one endpoint rather than proxying the traffic itself
Its Performance routing method directs each client to the endpoint with the lowest network latency
It can send requests for different URL paths to different endpoints
An existing TCP connection moves to a healthy endpoint immediately when the current endpoint fails a health check
why: Traffic Manager works purely at the DNS layer, resolving the profile name to the best endpoint and then stepping out of the path; Performance routing picks the lowest-latency endpoint for the client's source network. Because it never sees the HTTP request it cannot route by URL path, which is a layer-7 job for Application Gateway or Front Door. And since clients hold a cached DNS answer, failover only takes effect when the TTL expires and the client re-resolves; established connections are not redirected.

q: A company's on-premises network connects to Azure over an ExpressRoute circuit. During a rare ExpressRoute outage, they want traffic to automatically fail over to a site-to-site VPN connection instead of losing connectivity entirely. What should you do?
opts: Deploy a VPN gateway connection to the same virtual network, coexisting with the ExpressRoute connection
Nothing further, because an ExpressRoute circuit includes an automatic VPN fallback path
Migrate the circuit to Azure Virtual WAN, which fails over to the internet on its own
Enable zone-redundant gateways and ExpressRoute Direct for the circuit
why: ExpressRoute and site-to-site VPN connections can coexist on the same virtual network, and with both routes advertised the VPN path takes over when the circuit's routes disappear; this has to be deliberately configured, since nothing is created automatically. Virtual WAN also needs an explicit VPN connection before it can fail over to one. Zone-redundant gateways protect the gateway instances within a region, and ExpressRoute Direct is higher-bandwidth connectivity; neither provides an alternate path when the circuit itself is down.

q: A company already filters subnet traffic with NSGs but wants centralized, tenant-wide outbound filtering — for example, blocking outbound traffic to a specific list of known-malicious FQDNs — enforced consistently across many VNets from a single place to manage the rule set. Which is the better fit, and why doesn't relying on more NSGs solve this well?
opts: Azure Firewall, since it supports centralized FQDN-based filtering across multiple VNets from one managed instance
NSGs alone, since an NSG rule can already reference an FQDN directly as a destination
Azure Firewall, since NSGs are being fully retired and no longer supported on new subnets
NSGs alone, since adding one NSG per VNet is functionally identical to a centralized firewall
why: Azure Firewall supports FQDN-based filtering rules and is deployed once to centrally enforce policy across many VNets, matching the centralized, tenant-wide requirement here. NSGs filter by IP, port, and protocol — they don't support FQDN-based rules the way Azure Firewall does, and NSGs remain fully supported, not being retired. Reproducing the same rule set across many separate NSGs also isn't equivalent to one centrally managed policy — it means maintaining consistency across every one of them by hand.

q: An app team wants traffic from their subnet to a storage account to take an optimized path over the Microsoft backbone instead of the public internet, but the storage account itself can stay reachable at its existing public endpoint for other authorized callers. Which feature fits best?
opts: A service endpoint
A private endpoint
VNet peering
Azure Bastion
why: A service endpoint extends a subnet's identity onto the Microsoft backbone so traffic to the storage account takes an optimized route, while the storage account keeps its normal public endpoint reachable by other authorized callers. A private endpoint instead gives the storage account an actual private IP inside the VNet, changing how it's reached entirely rather than just optimizing the route. Peering connects two VNets to each other, not a VNet to a PaaS service, and Bastion is for RDP/SSH access to VMs, unrelated to storage connectivity.

q: If a route table on subnet A contains a 0.0.0.0/0 route whose next hop is a network virtual appliance, traffic between two VMs that are both in subnet A is also sent through the appliance.
opts: True
False
why: Routes are selected by longest prefix match, and the system route for the VNet's own address space is far more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so intra-subnet and intra-VNet traffic keeps going direct. Forcing that traffic through an appliance requires an explicit user-defined route for the VNet or subnet prefix with the appliance as next hop.

q: Which two of the following are benefits that DDoS Protection Standard adds on top of the Basic protection every Azure resource already gets automatically? (Choose two.)
opts: Attack analytics, metrics, and alerting tuned to the specific protected resource
Protection against common network-layer flood attacks
Cost protection credits for resource scale-out charges incurred during a documented attack
Automatic enrollment with no configuration or cost
why: DDoS Protection Standard (now DDoS Network Protection) adds resource-tuned attack analytics, metrics, and alerting, plus cost protection credits for scale-out charges incurred while defending against a documented attack — both are paid, Standard-only capabilities. Basic protection already covers common network-layer flood attacks for every resource at no cost, which is also why automatic, no-configuration, no-cost enrollment describes Basic, not something Standard adds on top of it.

q: You create a Standard SKU public IP address and associate it with the NIC of VM1, which runs Windows. The VM's subnet and NIC have no network security group. An administrator cannot connect over RDP from the internet. What should you do?
opts: Add a user-defined route with the next hop type Internet to the subnet
Create an NSG that allows inbound TCP 3389 and associate it with the NIC or subnet
Change the public IP address allocation from static to dynamic
Convert the public IP address to the Basic SKU
why: Standard SKU public IPs are secure by default, so inbound traffic is blocked until an NSG explicitly allows it; with no NSG, nothing is allowed. Standard addresses are static only, and the Basic SKU was retired on September 30, 2025. A route to the Internet is already the default for outbound and does not open inbound ports.

q: Several new subnets are created with the private subnet setting (defaultOutboundAccess disabled). VMs in them must reach the internet to download packages, and the team does not want a public IP on each VM. Which statement is correct, and what should you configure?
opts: The VMs have no implicit outbound path, so attach a NAT gateway to the subnets
Outbound access works once an NSG rule allows outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
The VMs use the default outbound IP, so no change is required
Outbound access works only if each VM is given a Basic SKU public IP
why: In a private subnet, Azure does not provide default outbound access, so VMs need an explicit method, and a NAT gateway shared by the subnet needs no public IP on the VMs. Relying on the default outbound IP is what the private subnet setting removes. The Basic SKU public IP is retired, and an NSG rule filters traffic but does not supply an outbound path.

q: VM1 has an NSG on its NIC with an inbound rule allowing TCP 443 from the internet. Clients still cannot connect on 443. The Effective security rules page for the NIC also shows a rule from the subnet's NSG at priority 200 that denies inbound TCP 443 from the internet. Why does the NIC-level allow have no effect?
opts: Allow rules in an NSG apply only to outbound traffic
A NIC NSG is ignored whenever a subnet NSG exists
Inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first, and the deny stops it before the NIC NSG is reached
The NIC NSG is evaluated first, and its allow is overridden by the higher-priority subnet NSG
why: For inbound traffic Azure applies the NSG on the subnet first, then the NSG on the NIC, and traffic must pass both. A deny in the subnet NSG ends the flow. The rules of the two NSGs are not merged by priority, a NIC NSG is never ignored, and allow rules apply to inbound traffic as well.

q: You need a one-time test from VM1 to a SQL endpoint on TCP 1433 that reports whether the connection works, the latency, and the hop where it fails. You do not need continuous monitoring. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?
opts: Connection troubleshoot
Packet capture
Connection monitor
Next hop
why: Connection troubleshoot runs a one-time connectivity check from a VM to a destination and reports reachability, latency, and the hop that fails. Connection monitor is the continuous, alert-capable service. Packet capture records packets for deeper analysis but does not test the path, and next hop only returns the routing decision for a destination.

q: You must start logging allowed and denied IP traffic for every workload in VNet1 and analyze it with Traffic Analytics. A colleague proposes creating NSG flow logs, but the portal will not allow it. What should you use instead?
opts: Azure Advisor network recommendations
Virtual network flow logs enabled on VNet1
A packet capture on every VM in the virtual network
Activity log diagnostic settings on the subscription
why: NSG flow logs are retiring on September 30, 2027 and can no longer be created, and virtual network flow logs are the replacement, enabled at the virtual network and covering its workloads. The activity log records control-plane operations, not traffic. Packet captures are short, per-VM diagnostics, and Advisor gives recommendations, not traffic logs.

q: A Standard internal load balancer has a TCP health probe on port 443. The application on the backend VMs listens on port 8443 only, and the Health Probe Status metric shows 0 percent for all instances although the VMs are running. What should you change?
opts: Increase the idle timeout of the load-balancing rule to ten minutes
Convert the Standard load balancer to the Basic SKU to relax probes
Add a public IP address to each of the backend VMs for probing
Change the health probe port to 8443 and align the backend port
why: A probe fails when nothing listens on the probed port, so the load balancer marks every instance unhealthy and stops sending traffic. Aligning the probe and backend port with the port the application uses fixes it. The Basic SKU is not a fix, backend VMs do not need public IPs for probes, and the idle timeout affects established flows, not health checks.

q: After a security review, an administrator adds an NSG rule at priority 4000 that denies all inbound traffic to the backend subnet, except 443 from the internet. Backend VMs for a Standard load balancer are now marked unhealthy even though the application is running and listening. What should you do?
opts: Change the load-balancing rule to use floating IP on the backend port
Disable the health probe so that all backend instances stay in rotation
Add an inbound allow rule for the AzureLoadBalancer tag below priority 4000
Delete the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule from the NSG so it is recreated
why: The default rule allowing the AzureLoadBalancer tag has priority 65001, so a custom deny at 4000 is processed first and blocks the probe source 168.63.129.16. An explicit allow with a lower priority number restores probing. Default rules cannot be deleted, floating IP does not affect probes, and disabling probes removes failover protection.

q: The root domain contoso.com must resolve to a Standard public IP address, and the address might change if the resource is recreated. A CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex. Which Azure DNS configuration meets the requirement?
opts: A CNAME record at the apex that targets the public IP's DNS label
An A record at the apex holding today's IP address, updated by hand
An NS record at the apex that points to the public IP address
An alias A record set at the apex that targets the public IP resource
why: An alias record set references the Azure resource itself and follows its address changes automatically, and alias A records are allowed at the apex. A CNAME at the apex is not valid DNS, a hand-maintained A record breaks whenever the address changes, and NS records delegate a zone and cannot point to an IP address.

q: A virtual network can be linked to several private DNS zones with auto registration enabled, so VMs register their records in all of them.
opts: True
False
why: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone with auto registration enabled. It can be linked to additional zones with registration disabled, where it can resolve records but does not register VMs automatically.

q: A compliance team requires that all RDP and SSH sessions made through Azure Bastion are recorded for later review, and that the host has no public IP address. Which Bastion SKU supports this?
opts: Standard
Developer
Basic
Premium
why: Session recording and private-only deployment are Premium features. Standard adds native client, shareable links, and scaling, but not recording. Basic offers browser access with two instances, and Developer is a free shared offering for one VM at a time.

q: You must receive an email within minutes whenever any virtual machine in resource group RG1 is deleted, including deletions performed through the CLI or a template. What should you create?
opts: An activity log alert for the Delete Virtual Machine operation at RG1 scope, with an action group
A metric alert rule on Percentage CPU with a threshold of 0 for the VMs in RG1
A log search alert rule on the Heartbeat table that fires when a VM in RG1 stops reporting
A Service Health alert rule for virtual machines in the region that contains RG1
why: Deleting a VM is a control-plane operation recorded in the activity log, and an activity log alert on that operation fires on every delete regardless of the tool used. The heartbeat query is the near-miss: a deleted VM does stop sending heartbeats, but so does a stopped, deallocated, or disconnected one, and the alert only fires after the missing-heartbeat window elapses. A deleted VM emits no metrics at all, so a CPU threshold never evaluates. Service Health reports Microsoft platform incidents, not actions taken in your subscription.

q: Fifty Windows VMs send their Security event log to a Log Analytics workspace through the Azure Monitor Agent. You must be alerted when event ID 4625 occurs more than 20 times in any 15-minute period on any single VM. Which type of alert rule should you create?
opts: A log search alert rule that queries the Event table, split by computer
A metric alert rule on the VMs with a dynamic threshold
An activity log alert rule filtered to the Security category
A Service Health alert rule with the Incident event type
why: Event IDs live in log data, so only a log search alert can count a specific ID per computer over a window and fire per VM using a dimension split. Metric alerts evaluate numeric time series such as CPU or disk; there is no metric for a Windows event ID. The activity log's Security category covers Defender for Cloud alerts about Azure resources, not events from inside a guest OS. Service Health alerts cover Azure platform incidents.

q: A company wants to be able to fail over an entire application's VMs to a secondary region if the primary region goes down entirely.
opts: A resource lock
Azure Advisor
Azure Backup alone
Azure Site Recovery
why: Site Recovery replicates and fails over whole workloads to a secondary region, unlike Backup, which restores point-in-time copies.

q: A user deleted a 2 GB folder from the data disk of VM1 yesterday. VM1 is protected by Azure Backup in a Recovery Services vault and must keep running. You need to recover only that folder with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opts: Use File Recovery on the recovery point to mount the disk and copy the folder back
Restore the recovery point to a new VM, then copy the folder across the network
Restore the recovery point as disks, attach them to VM1, and copy the folder
Use Azure Site Recovery to fail VM1 over to yesterday's recovery point
why: File Recovery generates a script that mounts the recovery point's disks over iSCSI directly on VM1 or another machine, so you browse to the folder and copy it, then unmount. Restoring a whole VM or restoring disks and attaching them both work, but they create extra resources, cost, and cleanup for 2 GB of data. Site Recovery replicates VMs to another region for disaster recovery; it is not a backup product and VM1 has no replica to fail over to.

q: An administrator is deploying monitoring to a fleet of new VMs and wants Microsoft's current, supported agent for collecting metrics and logs into Azure Monitor.
opts: The Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule
The legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA) with a workspace key
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) sending to a storage account
The Dependency agent on its own
why: The Azure Monitor Agent, configured through data collection rules, is the supported agent for new deployments. The Log Analytics agent was retired in August 2024 and should not be used for anything new. The Azure Diagnostics extension is an older collector aimed at storage accounts and Event Hubs, not Log Analytics. The Dependency agent only adds process and connection mapping for VM insights and depends on the Azure Monitor Agent being present.

q: A company needs a VM's resource logs both queryable right away in Log Analytics and archived cheaply for 7 years to satisfy a compliance requirement.
opts: One diagnostic setting that sends the logs to both a Log Analytics workspace and a storage account
Two diagnostic settings on the VM, because a diagnostic setting supports a single destination
Azure Backup of the VM with a seven-year retention rule in the vault policy
Continuous export from Microsoft Defender for Cloud to a storage account
why: A single diagnostic setting can fan the same logs out to several destinations at once, so one setting covers the workspace for querying and the storage account for cheap long-term archive. A second setting is unnecessary because the one-destination limit does not exist. Azure Backup protects disks, not the log stream. Continuous export from Defender for Cloud ships security alerts and recommendations, not a resource's own diagnostic logs.

q: An administrator needs to schedule recurring patch installation windows across dozens of Windows and Linux Azure VMs, and track patch compliance centrally.
opts: Azure Update Manager with a maintenance configuration
Azure Automation Update Management
Automatic VM guest patching enabled on each VM
An Azure Policy assignment with the DeployIfNotExists effect
why: Update Manager is the current service for assessing compliance across a fleet and installing updates in maintenance configurations you schedule. Automation Update Management is the near-miss: it did the same job, but it was retired in August 2024 along with the Log Analytics agent it depended on. Automatic guest patching installs updates during off-peak hours Azure chooses, with no administrator-defined window across the fleet. Policy can enforce that patch settings exist, but it does not orchestrate installations.

q: Soft delete for Azure Backup keeps deleted backup data recoverable for a retention window, even if someone deletes the backup item or disables backup entirely.
opts: True
False
why: This protection is distinct from blob soft delete and is designed to guard against accidental or malicious deletion of backup data itself, such as during a ransomware attack that disables backups.

q: An alert rule fires when a VM's CPU exceeds 90%. Which two of the following can the alert's action group do directly? (Choose two.)
opts: Start an Azure Automation runbook
Send a push notification to the Azure mobile app
Increase the instance count of a VM Scale Set
Restart the virtual machine without any additional resource
why: Action groups deliver notifications (email, SMS, voice, push) and invoke automation targets such as runbooks, Functions, Logic Apps, and webhooks. Changing a Scale Set's instance count is the job of autoscale rules, not alert actions; an alert can only reach a runbook that then calls the scale API. Likewise, restarting a VM is not a built-in action type, so it requires a runbook or Function to perform the restart.

q: A team wants to track end-to-end response times, failure rates, and dependency calls for a live web application, down to individual requests, not just VM-level metrics. Which Azure Monitor feature fits?
opts: Azure Service Health
Application Insights
Azure Advisor
Network Watcher
why: Application Insights is the Azure Monitor feature purpose-built for application performance monitoring — request rates, response times, failure rates, and dependency tracking down to individual requests. Service Health reports on Azure platform outages, Advisor gives configuration recommendations, and Network Watcher diagnoses network connectivity, none of which provide application-level performance telemetry.

q: Azure Backup's cross-region restore feature lets an administrator restore a VM into the paired secondary region, even while the primary region is fully available, provided the vault uses geo-redundant storage.
opts: True
False
why: Cross-region restore is specifically designed to let you restore into the secondary paired region on demand, for testing or migration purposes, not only during an actual regional outage, as long as the Recovery Services vault's storage redundancy is geo-redundant (GRS or RA-GRS) or geo-zone-redundant.

q: An administrator wants an email sent automatically whenever a VM's CPU usage stays above 90% for more than 10 minutes, without having to check the portal manually. Which Azure Monitor component should they configure?
opts: A metric alert rule with an action group that sends an email notification
Log Analytics, since it emails a daily summary of all metrics automatically
Azure Advisor, since it emails cost and performance recommendations weekly
Application Insights, configured to alert on high CPU for the application's App Service plan
why: A metric alert rule watches a specific metric like CPU percentage against a threshold and duration, and an action group defines what happens when it fires — including sending an email. Log Analytics stores and queries data but doesn't send scheduled summary emails on its own, Advisor gives periodic recommendations rather than real-time threshold alerts, and Application Insights is scoped to application-level telemetry, like an App Service plan's own metrics, not the CPU of an arbitrary VM.

q: A team enables a new Azure SQL Database and expects its detailed resource logs, like query performance insights, to start flowing into their existing Log Analytics workspace automatically. A week later, the workspace still shows nothing for that database. What's the most likely cause?
opts: No diagnostic setting was configured on the database to route its resource logs anywhere
Log Analytics workspaces only accept data from virtual machines, not platform services like Azure SQL Database
The workspace has reached its maximum data retention limit and is rejecting new data
Resource logs take a minimum of 30 days to begin appearing after a resource is created
why: Resource logs aren't sent anywhere by default — a diagnostic setting has to be explicitly configured on the resource to route its logs to a destination like a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an event hub. Log Analytics accepts data from many platform services, not just VMs; a workspace hitting its retention limit affects how long old data is kept, not whether new data is rejected; and there's no 30-day delay built into resource logging.

q: A team needs the Azure Monitor Agent to collect one specific custom Windows event log channel from a fleet of VMs and send it to their Log Analytics workspace, leaving out the noisier default channels they don't need. Which component defines exactly what gets collected and where it goes?
opts: A data collection rule associated with the VMs
A diagnostic setting on each VM
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) with a storage account sink
VM insights enabled on the VMs
why: A data collection rule tells the Azure Monitor Agent which data sources to collect, down to an XPath filter for one event channel, and which workspace to send them to. A diagnostic setting is the near-miss: it routes a resource's platform logs and metrics, but it has no view into the guest operating system's event logs. The Azure Diagnostics extension is the legacy collector aimed at storage accounts. VM insights deploys its own rule for performance counters and dependency maps, not custom event channels.

q: You need a KQL query against the SigninLogs table that returns, for the last 24 hours, the number of failed sign-ins per user and nothing else. Which two operators does the query require? (Choose two.)
opts: where
summarize
join
union
why: where narrows the rows to TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and ResultType != 0, and summarize count() by UserPrincipalName produces the per-user totals, which is the complete query. join and union both combine rows from more than one table or query, and only SigninLogs is involved here, so adding either would be unnecessary work at best.

q: You need to measure latency and packet loss every minute between web VMs in Azure and a database server in an on-premises datacenter that has Azure Arc enabled, and to be alerted when latency exceeds 100 ms. Which solution fits?
opts: A Service Health alert for the region that hosts the datacenter
Packet capture running continuously on each of the web VMs
IP flow verify on each web VM, scheduled with an Automation runbook
Connection monitor with an alert on its latency metric
why: Connection monitor provides continuous connectivity monitoring across Azure and hybrid endpoints, supports Arc-enabled servers as sources, measures latency and packet loss, and publishes metrics that can drive alert rules. IP flow verify only evaluates NSG rules for one flow. Packet capture is a short diagnostic recording. Service Health reports Microsoft platform incidents and says nothing about your path latency.

q: Maintenance on all VMs in rg-app happens every Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00. Dozens of alert rules cover those VMs, and the on-call team must not be paged during that window, but the alerts should still be recorded. What should you create?
opts: A Service Health alert that fires during the maintenance window
A new, empty action group that replaces the existing groups on every rule
An alert processing rule on rg-app that suppresses notifications weekly
A change to each alert rule so that it disables itself on Sunday nights
why: An alert processing rule can suppress action groups for a scope on a schedule, so alerts still fire and are recorded but notifications are not sent, and one rule covers all alert rules. Disabling rules one by one is slow and means nothing fires or is recorded. Replacing action groups changes every rule's behavior permanently, and a Service Health alert tells you about Azure incidents, not your maintenance.

q: Azure Backup alerts for all vaults in a subscription must trigger a single action group that opens an incident in the team's ITSM tool. Backup alerts do not offer an action group setting of their own. What should you configure?
opts: An alert processing rule that adds the action group in this subscription
Classic Azure Backup alert email settings configured on each vault
A new metric alert rule created on each of the Recovery Services vaults
A budget alert on the subscription that notifies the same action group
why: Alert processing rules can add an action group to alert types that have no action group setting of their own, such as Azure Backup alerts. A metric alert rule creates different alerts instead of routing the built-in ones, budget alerts track cost, and classic Azure Backup alerts were deprecated on March 31, 2026.

q: An alert processing rule that suppresses notifications prevents the alert from being created, so the alert does not appear in the alerts list.
opts: True
False
why: Alert processing rules modify alerts as they fire. Suppression removes the action groups, so no notification is sent, but the alert still fires and is recorded and visible in the alerts view. Disabling the alert rule is what prevents alerts from being generated.

q: Your company must protect Azure VMs, an Azure Files share, several Azure managed disks, and blobs in a storage account using Azure Backup in the same region. How many vault types do you need?
opts: A Backup vault for VMs and files, and a Recovery Services vault for disks and blobs
A Recovery Services vault for VMs and files, and a Backup vault for disks and blobs
A single Backup vault that holds the backups for all four data sources
A single Recovery Services vault that holds the backups for all four data sources
why: Recovery Services vaults hold VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises workloads, while Backup vaults hold newer data sources such as Azure Disks and Azure Blobs, so both types are needed. No single vault type covers all four, and the pairing that puts VMs and files in a Backup vault reverses which vault holds what.

q: A backup administrator needs reports that show backup usage trends, job success, and storage consumed across 12 Recovery Services vaults in 3 subscriptions over the last 6 months. What must be configured to get them?
opts: A Cost analysis view filtered to the vaults and grouped by resource group
An Azure Advisor recommendation enabled on each of the vaults with weekly emails
A resource lock on each vault, combined with an activity log alert on it
Diagnostic settings sending vault data to a Log Analytics workspace, then Backup reports
why: Backup reports use Azure Monitor logs and workbooks, so each vault's diagnostic settings must send data to a Log Analytics workspace, which can collect from vaults across subscriptions. Advisor gives recommendations, Cost analysis reports spending rather than job success, and a lock protects the vault but does not collect data.

q: VMs in the primary region failed over to the secondary region using Azure Site Recovery. The primary region is available again, and you want the VMs in the secondary region to start replicating back to the primary region so you can fail back later. What should you do?
opts: Run a failover using the Custom recovery point
Reprotect the failed-over VMs
Delete the replicated items and enable replication again from scratch
Run a test failover on the failed-over VMs
why: After a failover, reprotecting the VMs makes them replicate from the secondary region back toward the original region, which prepares a failback. A test failover creates a copy in an isolated network and starts nothing in reverse. Deleting items loses the replication relationship, and another failover is the wrong direction.

q: An application tier is replicated with Azure Site Recovery. During a drill, the business says it can accept no more than a few seconds of data loss, even if recovery takes several minutes longer. Which recovery point should you choose when failing over?
opts: Latest
Latest app-consistent
Latest processed
Custom
why: Latest processes all data already sent to Site Recovery before creating the VM, so it gives the lowest recovery point objective at the price of more time. Latest processed fails over immediately using the newest processed point, giving the lowest recovery time but possibly more data loss. App-consistent points are taken less often, and Custom is a manual choice for one VM.

q: Azure Site Recovery raises a health issue when no successful test failover has been run for a protected VM in the last 180 days.
opts: True
False
why: Site Recovery expects a successful test failover at least once every 180 days and raises a failover-readiness health issue if none exists or the latest one is older. Regular drills confirm that failover will work before an outage.

q: You need one view that shows capacity, transactions, availability, and latency across 30 storage accounts in several resource groups, with the ability to drill into a hotspot. Which tool should you use?
opts: VM insights in Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
Network Insights in Azure Monitor
Storage insights in Azure Monitor
why: Storage insights gives a unified at-scale view of Azure Storage accounts, including capacity, availability, transactions, and latency, with drill-down. Network Insights covers network resources, VM insights covers the performance and dependencies of VMs, and Service Health reports on Azure platform incidents.

q: Which two statements about retention of Azure Monitor data are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The Activity log is kept for 90 days
Platform metrics are stored for 93 days with no configuration needed
Resource logs are collected automatically and kept for 93 days
Platform metrics are kept for 30 days unless a workspace is attached
why: Platform metrics are collected automatically and stored for 93 days, and the Activity log is retained for 90 days. Resource logs are not collected until a diagnostic setting sends them to a destination, and metrics do not depend on a workspace for their standard retention.

q: The following KQL query is run against a Log Analytics workspace: Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | summarize count() by Computer. What does it return?
opts: Each computer that sent a heartbeat in the last 15 minutes, with its heartbeat count
A time chart showing heartbeat counts per computer in 15-minute bins
Every computer that has ever sent a heartbeat, with the total count since onboarding
Only the computers that missed every heartbeat in the last 15 minutes
why: where filters the rows to the last 15 minutes, and summarize count() by Computer returns one row per computer with the number of heartbeats in that window. It does not look at older data, it cannot list computers with no rows because they do not appear in the table, and without bin() or render it does not produce time bins or a chart.
